sales_orders.title: Selling 4 — Sales Orders
sales_orders.desc: Sales Orders in ZhiftERP: the field walk — header pre-fill, the customer's PO reference, per-row delivery dates, the items table checked against the accepted version, and the payment schedule table; the commitment mechanics — stock reservation into the Bin, the credit check at submission, the execution basis with %delivered and %billed, and the order confirmation; wave scheduling against projected stock with the weekly planning read; the amendment discipline — the change taxonomy, the controlled lanes, cancellations and the Closed status, and the monthly amendments read; milestone payment schedules with advances requested, received against the order, and allocated at invoicing; and the order book's six reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Sales Order: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Sales Order in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Sales Order field walk; state what submission commits and reserves; plan per-row delivery schedules including multi-wave orders; operate the amendment and cancellation discipline; configure payment schedules and handle advances; and run the order book reads.

What a Sales Order is. The Sales Order is the agreement: the business commits to supply these items, in these quantities, at these prices, on this schedule, on these payment terms. Everything before it was offer (module 3); everything after it executes it — the Delivery Notes ship against it (module 5), the invoices bill against it (module 7), the stock reserves for it, and the credit exposure counts it. The order is therefore the document the business is held to, and this module's disciplines exist because an incorrectly stated commitment is costly to correct.

Order sources.

1. Conversion from a quotation — the enterprise and negotiated lane (module 3, Chapter 7): the order inherits the final accepted version with its evidence.
2. Direct entry — the routine trade lane: standing customers ordering from the lists, entered against the registers with no quotation required per the policy. Direct orders carry the same disciplines — pre-filled rates, the units read, credit checked — with the customer's purchase order reference attached where one exists.

What submission does. Stated here and detailed in Chapter 3: the order's quantities enter the reserved figures the stock system carries; the credit check runs against the customer's limit; the delivery and billing machinery gains its basis; and the order joins the order book the business plans from. An unsubmitted draft commits nothing; a submitted order commits everything it states.

Custody. The sales function enters and maintains orders; commercial changes re-enter the deviation ladder (module 3's bands apply to order amendments exactly as to offers); schedule changes follow the amendment procedure; and the standing rule: the order states the whole agreement — nothing is promised beside it, and nothing on it changes without its documented amendment.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: the commitment mechanics. Chapter 4: the delivery schedule. Chapter 5: amendments and cancellations. Chapter 6: the payment schedule and advances. Chapter 7: the order book reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Sales Order doctype
lessons.html:
Open Sales Order (awesome bar) > New — or arrive here by conversion from a quotation. Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Customer and the header pre-fill. The customer selection pulls module 1's machinery: currency, price list, payment terms template, addresses, contact. On converted orders the quotation's values carry; the verification rule stands either way — the header is read before the rows.

2. Customer's Purchase Order. The customer's own PO number and date, entered where the customer issues one (enterprise and institutional customers almost always do). The reference prints on the delivery and invoice documents, and the customer's payables function matches against it — a missing PO reference is a payment delay at the customer's end.

3. Delivery Date. The header delivery date, and — the field that matters for real schedules — the per-row delivery dates in the items table: each row carries its own date, which is how one order states a multi-wave schedule (Chapter 4). The header date is the latest commitment; the rows state the plan.

4. The items table. Per row: item, quantity, UOM (the unit column read, per module 2's discipline), rate (inherited from the quotation or pre-filled from the lists; deviations per the ladder), amount, the per-row delivery date, and the source warehouse where the site sets it at order time. Converted orders are checked row-by-row against the final quotation version — the module 3 handoff's receiving side.

5. Taxes and Charges. Per the template, as quoted. The order's tax total is the invoice's tax total; discrepancies trace to template or classification errors and are fixed at the source, not edited on the document.

6. Payment Terms Schedule. The terms template generates the schedule table — due dates and portions (Chapter 6). Milestone structures (the advance-delivery-completion split) are entered here as the schedule the invoices will follow.

7. Terms, source, and attachments. The T&C as quoted; the source quotation linked (conversion does this); the acceptance evidence attached (module 3, Chapter 7) — the customer's PO document, the signed offer. The order file is the agreement file.

8. Save, review, submit. Draft review per the value threshold (the preparer/reviewer split on commitments above the band); submission runs the credit check and commits the order (Chapter 3).

Verification per order. Header read; rows against the accepted version or the lists; units read; per-row dates stating the real plan; the schedule per the agreed terms; evidence attached; then submit — and the order confirmation to the customer per Chapter 3.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The commitment mechanics
lessons.html:
Submission turns a draft into a commitment. This chapter is exactly what commits, where it shows, and the confirmation that closes the loop.

1. Stock reservation. Each submitted row's undelivered quantity enters the Reserved Qty on the item-warehouse Bin (the Inventory track, module 1, Chapter 6). The consequences:

1. Projected quantity falls — replenishment arithmetic sees the commitment: the reorder machinery orders against promised stock, not just shelf stock.
2. Availability questions answer honestly — the next order's preparer sees projected, not actual, and does not promise the same stock twice.
3. Reservation hygiene matters — the stale-order reservations the Inventory track's monthly read hunts (orders that will never fulfil, holding stock on paper) are this module's Chapter 7 hygiene, read from the selling side.

2. The credit check. Submission tests outstanding exposure plus this order against the customer's limit (module 1, Chapter 5): the block posture refuses the over-limit order; the named bypass role may pass it as a listed decision. The order is where credit exposure is created — the invoice merely documents what the order committed . For this reason the check runs at submission and not only at invoicing.

3. The execution basis. The submitted order becomes the reference every downstream document draws from:

1. Delivery Notes create from the order, drawing rows and quantities (module 5) — the %delivered figure tracks fulfilment per row.
2. Sales Invoices bill against the order per the payment schedule (module 7) — the %billed figure tracks it.
3. The two percentages together state the order's life at a glance: delivered and billed to completion is a closed commitment; the gaps between them are Chapter 7's reads.

4. The order confirmation. After submission, the confirmation goes to the customer per the policy: the order document (the site's print format) stating what was agreed — items, quantities, prices, schedule, terms. The confirmation is the final opportunity to catch a disagreement before execution: the customer reads their own commitment back and finds any wrong quantity or date now, against a document, rather than at delivery. Enterprise orders confirm as standing procedure; routine trade confirms per the policy's threshold.

5. What submission does not do. It does not move stock (deliveries do), does not create receivables (invoices do), and does not collect the advance (the payment entry does, Chapter 6). The order is the promise; the downstream documents are the performance — and keeping the two distinct is what lets the reads in Chapter 7 say precisely where any order stands.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The delivery schedule
lessons.html:
Real orders ship in waves. This chapter is the scheduling machinery and its planning reads.

1. Per-row delivery dates. The items table carries a delivery date per row — the mechanism for every schedule shape:

1. The single-wave order — all rows on one date; the header date matches.
2. The multi-wave order — the same item split across rows with different dates (100 units on the first date, 100 on the second), or different items on different dates per the plan. The rows state the schedule; the header carries the final date.
3. The rule: the rows state the real plan agreed with the customer, not a placeholder — every planning read below computes from these dates, and a schedule entered as one optimistic date produces overdue flags on stock the customer never expected yet.

2. Scheduling against stock. The order's dates are checked against availability at entry: projected quantity per item per warehouse (the Inventory track's figure) against each wave's quantity and date, with incoming purchase schedules visible where the site exposes them. A wave the stock cannot meet is a conversation at order time — the date moved, the quantity split, or the replenishment expedited — not a discovery at picking. For orders that drive procurement (the enterprise order requiring equipment purchase), the procurement lane is triggered from the order per the site's flow, and the wave dates account for the supplier's lead time.

3. Wave execution. Each wave ships as its own Delivery Note against the order (module 5's territory): the note draws the wave's rows and quantities, the %delivered figure advances, and the remaining rows hold their dates. The order remains the single reference across all waves — one agreement, several performances, each documented.

4. The delivery planning read — weekly. Open order rows by delivery date:

1. The coming window — rows due in the planning horizon, grouped by warehouse and route: the picking and despatch workload, visible a week out.
2. The overdue rows — rows past their date and undelivered: each is a commitment the business is currently missing, chased to its cause (stock, transport, a customer hold) and either delivered or re-dated by documented amendment with the customer's agreement (Chapter 5). An overdue row left unexplained is the read failing at its purpose.
3. The at-risk rows — due rows whose projected stock is short: flagged before their date, while the expedite-or-re-date conversation is still cheap.

5. Schedule changes. Dates move — customers defer, stock delays. Every date movement is an amendment per Chapter 5's procedure: the row's date updated through the amendment lane with the reason and the customer's agreement noted. The schedule's history then reads honestly: what was promised, what moved, why, and with whose agreement — which is the record the service-level conversation at year-end is conducted from.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Amendments and cancellations
lessons.html:
Agreements change; the record must change correctly. This chapter is the discipline.

1. The change taxonomy. Changes route by what they touch:

1. Commercial changes — rates, discounts, added lines at negotiated prices: these re-enter module 3's deviation ladder at the band the change belongs to. An order amendment does not bypass the offer's approvals; the concession that was never approved does not become approved by appearing on an amendment.
2. Quantity changes — increases run the credit and availability checks again (more commitment); decreases release reservation and are checked against work already done (a wave already picked or shipped does not un-ship by amendment — the return lane in module 5 handles physical reversals).
3. Schedule changes — date movements per Chapter 4.5: documented, reasoned, agreed.
4. Administrative changes — references, contacts, addresses for undelivered waves: ordinary edits with notes.

2. The amendment mechanics. Submitted orders change through the site's controlled lanes:

1. The update facility for submitted orders — quantity and schedule updates on undelivered rows, permitted to the roles the matrix names, each update logged by the system. This is the standard lane for the common cases.
2. Cancel-and-amend — the full amendment for structural changes: the order cancels with its reason and the amended version issues carrying the reference, per the standing document rules. Downstream documents already submitted against the order gate what cancellation is possible — an order with deliveries posted amends around its performed portion.
3. Either lane, the same records rule: the change, the reason, the approver per the taxonomy, and the customer's agreement where the agreement moved — on the document trail, not in a phone call's memory.

3. Cancellations. The order that will not proceed cancels with its reason code (customer cancelled, credit refused, superseded), releasing its reservations and closing its schedule rows. Cancellation reasons are a small defined set, per the standing reason-code pattern, because the quarterly cancellations read aggregates them into a why. Partial situations — some waves shipped, the remainder cancelled — close the undelivered rows per the procedure, leaving the performed portion intact and billed.

4. The status vocabulary. The order's status states its life: To Deliver and Bill, To Bill, To Deliver, Completed, Cancelled, Closed. Closed is the deliberate early end: the customer takes no more against this order, remaining quantities release, the record preserves what happened. Closing is a decision with a reason, used at the stale-order hygiene read (Chapter 7) — the alternative, orders left open forever at partial delivery, is the misstated order book Chapter 9 lists among the errors.

5. The amendments read — monthly. Orders amended in the month: the change, the lane, the approver, reconciled against the taxonomy's requirements — commercial changes carrying ladder approvals, schedule changes carrying agreements. The sibling of every fields-move-by-decision read in the programme, applied to commitments.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The payment schedule and advances
lessons.html:
The order states when money is due, and enterprise orders collect part of it before work starts. This chapter is the machinery.

1. The payment schedule table. The order's Payment Terms section: the template (module 1, Chapter 5) generates the schedule rows — each a portion and a due basis. Structures the schedule expresses:

1. The standing terms case — one row: 100% due at the term's interval from invoice.
2. The milestone case — the enterprise pattern: an advance portion due at order, a portion due on delivery, a retention portion due at completion (the 50/40/10 shape). Each row's portion and timing enter as the negotiated agreement states, and the invoices (module 7) follow the schedule as their billing plan.

2. Advances against orders. The advance portion collects before delivery:

1. The request — the payment request against the order for the advance portion, sent per the policy (the enterprise order does not enter the work queue until the advance clears, where the terms say so — the schedule is enforced, not decorative).
2. The receipt — the Payment Entry recording the customer's payment against the Sales Order as an advance: the entry references the order, the money lands in the bank account, and the customer's balance shows the advance held.
3. The allocation — when the invoices raise (module 7), the advance allocates against them per the schedule: the advance held becomes payment applied, and the customer's statement reads coherently — order, advance, invoice, allocation. An advance received but never allocated is a reconciliation item the receivables read surfaces; the allocation step is part of the invoicing procedure, not an afterthought.

3. Custody and the accounting boundary. The sales function agrees the schedule (within the terms the ladder approved) and tracks the milestones; the accounts function receives, records, and allocates the money per the Accounts track's procedures. The boundary rule: sales confirms what is due when; accounts confirms what arrived and where it applied — and the order's schedule is the shared reference both read from.

4. The schedule reads.

1. The advance status read — weekly on the enterprise book: orders whose schedule requires an advance, against advances received — the unfunded order that entered the work queue is the finding.
2. The milestone read — monthly: due milestones against invoicing and collection: the delivered wave whose delivery-portion invoice never raised, the completed order whose retention was never billed. Both are revenue sitting unbilled through process gaps, and module 7's invoicing discipline consumes this read.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The order book reads
lessons.html:
The open orders are the business's committed future. This chapter is the reads that keep the book true and worked.

1. The order book — weekly. All open orders with value, age, %delivered, %billed, and next scheduled date. The book is the selling function's working list and the owner's forward view: committed revenue, its schedule, and its execution state in one report. The weekly pass works it top-down by value: the largest commitments' next actions confirmed on calendar.

2. The overdue-delivery read — weekly (Chapter 4's read, restated as the book's column). Rows past date, each with its cause and its action — delivered, expedited, or re-dated by documented amendment. The read's output is a short list of rows, each with a named owner and action.

3. The delivered-not-billed read — weekly. Orders (and waves) where %delivered leads %billed beyond the invoicing cadence: performance the business has given away without yet asking for its money. Module 7 owns the invoicing procedure; this read is the order-side alarm that feeds it, and its target state is a list that clears at each invoicing run.

4. The billed-not-delivered read — monthly. The inverse gap: invoicing ahead of delivery beyond the advance structure the schedule authorises. Legitimate cases trace to their schedule rows (the advance invoice per the milestone plan); the remainder are errors to correct before they become customer disputes.

5. The stale-order hygiene read — monthly. Open orders with no movement (no delivery, no invoice, no amendment) across the policy's window:

1. The reservation cost stated — each stale order holds Reserved Qty against stock other orders could use (Chapter 3; the Inventory track reads the same figure from the other side).
2. The action per order — revived with a real schedule (the customer confirms new dates by amendment), or Closed with its reason, releasing the reservation.
3. The target — a book containing only live commitments, because every planning figure downstream (projected stock, committed revenue, the delivery workload) computes from it.

6. The cancellations and closures read — quarterly. The quarter's cancelled and closed orders by reason code: the distribution goes to the owner as data (credit refusals rising, customer cancellations concentrated in a segment, closures from stock failure), with the orders named, per the standing rule.

7. The filing. The book and its reads file with the sales records; the order file per order — the agreement, evidence, amendments, waves, schedule — remains the one-lookup answer for any commitment's history, and module 7 will add the invoicing and collection layers onto the same file.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the Montaigne AH order
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through the order that module 3's negotiation produced. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — creation from the accepted version (Chapter 2). The order creates from round two — the final accepted quotation — and is checked row-by-row against it: the 12-branch equipment lines with the 4% terminal concession intact (terminals only, per the approval's named scope; scanners and printers at list), installation and training as restructured in round two. Montaigne AH's purchase order number enters the header; the acceptance document attaches. The header is read; the rows are read; the units are read.

Step 2 — the schedule entered (Chapters 2, 4, 6).

1. Delivery: the rollout plan enters as per-row dates in three waves — the first branches in the first wave, the remainder across the following two, each row carrying its wave's date; the header carries the final date.
2. Payment: the negotiated milestone structure enters as the schedule table — 50% advance at order, 40% on delivery, 10% at completion — the rows stating portion and basis exactly as the agreement reads.

Step 3 — one change at signature (Chapter 5). Montaigne AH requests one change as they sign: the training component moves to sit after the second delivery wave rather than the first. The change is classified per the taxonomy: a schedule change with no commercial movement — the training row's date amends through the standard lane with the reason and the customer's agreement noted. No re-quote, no ladder: the taxonomy routed it in one step.

Step 4 — submission and the commitments (Chapter 3). Submission reserves the equipment quantities (projected stock at the fulfilling warehouse falls by the order — the procurement lane for the hardware was triggered at conversion, its lead time inside wave one's date), passes the credit check at the customer's limit, and issues the order confirmation. The confirmation step performs its function: Montaigne AH's operations team confirms the branch sequence against their own rollout plan before anything ships.

Step 5 — the advance (Chapter 6). The advance request issues for the 50% portion; the Payment Entry records receipt against the order; the enterprise book's advance read shows the order funded before the work queue takes it. The advance will allocate against the wave invoices per the schedule as module 7 raises them.

Step 6 — the book carries it (Chapter 7). The order book shows the commitment at value with its three-wave schedule; the weekly planning read carries wave one into the picking horizon; %delivered and %billed sit at zero, ready to advance as module 5 ships wave one. The order file — agreement, evidence, the one amendment, the schedule, the advance — answers the commitment in one lookup, and modules 5 and 7 will write the performance onto it.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in Sales Orders, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the promise beside the order. Symptom: commitments made in calls and messages that the order does not state; deliveries and disputes referencing agreements no document carries. Correction: the real agreement amended onto the order with its approvals. Prevention: the standing rule — the order states the whole agreement, and the confirmation puts it in the customer's hands.

Error 2 — the placeholder schedule. Symptom: one optimistic header date on multi-wave reality; overdue flags on rows the customer never expected; planning reads computing from fiction. Correction: the rows re-dated to the real plan by amendment. Prevention: per-row dates stating the agreed schedule at entry.

Error 3 — the amendment bypass. Symptom: commercial concessions appearing via amendment without ladder approval; the offer's controls bypassed after acceptance. Correction: the amendments read catches it; the change re-enters the ladder or reverses. Prevention: the change taxonomy — commercial changes re-ladder, always.

Error 4 — reservations held by dead orders. Symptom: stale orders reserving stock for months; projected figures misleading replenishment and availability answers. Correction: the hygiene read — revive with real dates or Close with reason. Prevention: the monthly read and the Closed status used as the decision it is.

Error 5 — the unenforced schedule. Symptom: advance terms on paper, work starting unfunded; milestones passing unbilled. Correction: the advance and milestone reads run; the unbilled portions invoiced. Prevention: the schedule enforced — the work queue gated on the advance where terms say so, and module 7 billing from the schedule.

Error 6 — the silent date slip. Symptom: delivery dates moved in place without reasons or customer agreement; the schedule's history unreadable; service-level reviews with no documentary record. Correction: the movements documented retroactively where evidence allows. Prevention: every date movement an amendment with reason and agreement noted.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the field walk including the customer PO reference, per-row dates, and the schedule table; state submission's four effects and what it does not do; plan waves against stock with the weekly planning read; route changes by the taxonomy through the controlled lanes with the amendments read; operate the milestone schedule with advances requested, received against the order, and allocated at invoicing; and run the order book's six reads.

Module rule 4: the Sales Order states the whole agreement — created from the accepted version or the registers, committing stock and credit at submission, scheduled per row as the real plan, changed only through the taxonomy's lanes with approvals and agreement, funded per its payment schedule, and kept live by the book's reads. Module 5 covers Delivery Notes and returns.

delivery.title: Selling 5 — Delivery Notes & Returns
delivery.desc: Delivery Notes and returns in ZhiftERP: the field walk — shipping addresses per despatch, honest posting dates, source warehouses, identity on controlled rows, and the order reference; the picking and despatch procedure with the pick list, identity capture at pick, second-person verification, submission at despatch, and the acknowledgment; partial rows and wave execution under the one-document-per-destination rule with the over-delivery tolerance; the four postings of submission and the three correction lanes; the return lane — the return document from the original, the identity check, reason codes, the condition decision including the pharmaceutical saleability ruling, and the credit-note tie; and the six delivery reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Delivery Note: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Delivery Note and sales returns in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Delivery Note field walk; run the picking and despatch procedure with its verification step; execute partial and wave deliveries against order rows; state what submission posts to stock and accounting; process returns through the return lane with the condition decision; and run the delivery reads.

What a Delivery Note is. The Delivery Note records a physical despatch of goods to a customer: which items, in what quantities, from which warehouse, to which address, on which date. It is the document of custody transfer — before submission the goods are the business's stock; after submission they are the customer's goods — and it is the delivery evidence every later question refers to: what shipped, when, with which serial and batch numbers, and who signed for it.

Position in the flow. The Delivery Note sits between the Sales Order and the Sales Invoice:

1. It is created from the order — the order states the commitment; the Delivery Note records the portion of it performed in this despatch. Direct Delivery Notes without orders are permitted only where the policy allows them (routine trade per the site's configuration); the standing pattern is order first.
2. It advances %delivered — the order's fulfilment figure computes from submitted Delivery Notes.
3. It feeds invoicing — module 7 bills delivered quantities per the payment schedule; the delivered-not-billed read (module 4, Chapter 7) measures the gap.

What submission does, stated in advance. Chapter 5 covers the postings in detail. In summary: stock leaves the warehouse (Stock Ledger Entries), cost of goods sold posts under perpetual inventory, and the reserved quantity for the delivered portion releases. A submitted Delivery Note is therefore a stock and accounting event, and the disciplines in this module exist to ensure the event matches the physical despatch exactly.

Custody. The warehouse function picks and despatches; a second person verifies the picked goods against the document before submission; the sales function monitors fulfilment through the reads; and the standing rule for the module: the Delivery Note states what physically left, with its identity, verified before submission and acknowledged at receipt.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: picking and despatch. Chapter 4: partial and wave deliveries. Chapter 5: what submission posts. Chapter 6: returns. Chapter 7: the delivery reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Delivery Note doctype
lessons.html:
Create the Delivery Note from the Sales Order (Create > Delivery Note) so the rows, rates, and references carry over. Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Customer and addresses. The customer carries from the order. Verify two addresses:

1. The shipping address — the destination of this despatch. On multi-site customers (module 1, Chapter 4) each Delivery Note selects the receiving branch's address; the address prints on the despatch paperwork the driver carries.
2. The billing address — carried for the invoice linkage; it does not change per despatch.

2. Posting Date and Time. The date and time the goods physically leave. The honest-date rule from the Inventory track applies: the Delivery Note posts when the despatch happens, on the date it happens.

3. The items table. Rows draw from the order:

1. Quantity per row — the quantity in this despatch, up to the row's remaining undelivered quantity. Chapter 4 covers partial rows.
2. UOM — as ordered; the unit column is read per the standing discipline.
3. Source Warehouse — the warehouse the goods leave. It must be the warehouse the goods physically leave; a Delivery Note posting from one warehouse while goods leave another corrupts both warehouses' balances.
4. Serial and batch numbers — controlled items carry their identity on the rows through the bundle (Inventory track, module 3): the delivered batch and serial numbers are the record the recall trace, the warranty file, and any later dispute read from.
5. Rate and amount — carried from the order for the invoice linkage; the Delivery Note does not renegotiate prices.

4. Transporter details. Where the site uses them: the transporter, vehicle, and driver fields per the despatch procedure. These fields identify the carrier leg for the transit-damage read (Chapter 7).

5. Order reference. The linked Sales Order per row — created-from carries it. The reference is what advances %delivered and what the invoice will draw on.

6. Save, verify, submit. The Delivery Note is saved as a draft for the verification step (Chapter 3), and submitted at the moment of despatch. Submission posts the stock and accounting events (Chapter 5); after submission, corrections follow the document rules — cancel and amend with cause, or the return lane where goods have physically moved (Chapter 6).

Verification per document. The shipping address is the destination; the posting date is the despatch date; each row's quantity, unit, and warehouse match the physical goods; identity numbers are complete on controlled rows; the order reference is present.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Picking and despatch
lessons.html:
The procedure between the planning read and the departing vehicle. Each step has an owner and a record.

1. The pick list. The weekly planning read (module 4, Chapter 4) provides the rows due in the window. Per despatch, the pick list states: the order reference, the items, the quantities in their units, the source warehouse locations, and the identity requirements for controlled items. The picker works from the list, not from memory of the order.

2. Picking.

1. Pick against the list — item, quantity, unit, per line; part-quantities counted in units per the unit-column discipline.
2. Capture identity at pick — for batch-controlled items, the picked batch is the batch recorded (first-expiry-first-out per the Inventory track's picking rule); for serialised items, the physical serial numbers of the picked units are scanned or recorded. The identity on the document must be the identity in the carton; the Inventory track's rule that the document names what was physically picked applies here in full.
3. Stage the picked goods — at the despatch area (the dispatch-bay warehouse where the site uses one), separated per destination.

3. The verification step. Before submission, a second person checks the staged goods against the draft Delivery Note: line count, quantities in the stated units, identity numbers against the physical labels, destination address against the load plan. The check is recorded (the checker's confirmation per the site's procedure). This step exists because the Delivery Note becomes the custody and accounting record at submission, and an error caught at the bay costs minutes while an error discovered at the customer costs a return cycle.

4. Despatch and submission. The Delivery Note submits when the goods physically leave — the same-time standard. The despatch pack travels with the goods: the printed Delivery Note (the site's standard format), and the documents the destination requires. For inter-city despatches the transporter fields are completed before departure.

5. The acknowledgment. The customer's receipt is recorded:

1. The signed copy — the customer (or the receiving branch) signs the Delivery Note copy; the signed copy or its scan attaches to the document as the proof of delivery.
2. Discrepancies at receipt — the customer's count differing from the document is recorded on the acknowledgment at the point of delivery, and the discrepancy routes to the corrective lane the same day: the short line investigated (the pick error, the transit loss) and corrected by its proper document, never by an informal adjustment.
3. The pending-acknowledgment read (Chapter 7) lists deliveries without signed copies; the target is a complete file, because the acknowledgment is the document that settles a delivery dispute.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Partial and wave deliveries
lessons.html:
Orders fulfil in parts. This chapter covers the mechanics of partial rows, wave execution, and the tolerance settings.

1. Partial rows. A Delivery Note row may carry less than the order row's quantity:

1. The delivered quantity posts; the remainder stays open on the order row with its date.
2. %delivered advances by the delivered portion.
3. Subsequent Delivery Notes draw the remaining quantity until the row completes.

Partial delivery is a normal mechanism, not an exception — the schedule's waves (module 4) and stock timing both use it. The requirement is that each partial despatch is a complete document in itself: verified, identified, acknowledged.

2. Wave execution. A multi-wave order (per-row delivery dates, module 4, Chapter 4) executes as one Delivery Note per despatch event:

1. One Delivery Note per vehicle-load per destination — the same rule as internal transfers (Inventory track, module 2): the receiving count matches one physical event.
2. The wave's rows only — the Delivery Note draws the rows and quantities due in this wave; later waves' rows remain on the order with their dates.
3. Multi-destination waves — a wave serving several branches produces one Delivery Note per branch, each with its own shipping address, verification, and acknowledgment. The order remains the single commitment reference across all of them.

3. Over-delivery tolerance. Stock Settings and the selling configuration carry the over-delivery allowance: the percentage by which a delivered quantity may exceed the ordered quantity before the system refuses the row. The standing posture is a low tolerance with the exception role named (the Inventory track, module 8 records the setting in the control register). The tolerance exists for genuine packing arithmetic (the carton that rounds a quantity), not as a licence to ship unordered goods; deliveries beyond it require the order amended first, through module 4's amendment lanes.

4. Delivery against sufficient stock. The Delivery Note posts from actual stock. With Allow Negative Stock off (the standing posture), a despatch the warehouse balance cannot cover does not submit — which surfaces, at despatch time, either a picking error (the goods came from a different warehouse than the document states) or a records error (a movement was never posted). Both are corrected by their proper documents before the delivery proceeds; the refusal is the control operating as designed.

5. The completion of a row and an order. A row completes when its delivered quantity equals its ordered quantity (within tolerance). An order completes when all rows complete and billing completes (module 7). Rows the customer will no longer take are closed through module 4's amendment or closure procedures — they do not remain open indefinitely, per the stale-order hygiene read.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — What submission posts
lessons.html:
Submission converts the verified document into stock and accounting events. This chapter states each posting and its consequence.

1. The stock posting. Per row, a Stock Ledger Entry: the quantity leaves the source warehouse at the item's valuation rate (the Inventory track, module 5 — the method's rate, never a typed rate). Consequences:

1. The warehouse balance falls; the Bin updates.
2. For controlled items, the batch and serial balances fall per the bundle — the delivered identities are recorded as delivered, which is what makes the downstream recall trace and the warranty record possible.
3. The stock is no longer the business's: the custody transfer is effective at submission.

2. The accounting posting. Under perpetual inventory: the stock account credits and cost of goods sold debits, at the valuation the stock ledger computed. This is the cost side of the sale's margin; the revenue side posts when the Sales Invoice submits (module 7). The two postings are deliberately separate documents because delivery and invoicing are separate events with separate dates, and the delivered-not-billed read measures the interval between them.

3. The reservation release. The delivered quantity leaves Reserved Qty on the Bin: the commitment recorded at order submission (module 4, Chapter 3) is performed to that extent, and projected quantities update accordingly.

4. The order update. %delivered advances on the linked order; the row's remaining quantity reduces; the order's status moves per the status vocabulary when thresholds are reached.

5. Corrections after submission. The correction lane depends on whether goods physically moved:

1. Goods did not leave (the despatch was cancelled after submission): the Delivery Note cancels with its reason; the stock and accounting postings reverse; the order rows reopen. The cancellation is same-day, because a submitted Delivery Note for goods still on the shelf misstates both custody and cost for as long as it stands.
2. Goods left and must come back: the return lane (Chapter 6) — a new document recording the physical return, never a cancellation of the despatch that genuinely happened.
3. A field error on a correct despatch (a wrong reference, a missing transporter detail): the administrative correction per the document rules, with the note.

6. The posting verification. Riding the Inventory track's monthly tie-out: Delivery Note postings are part of the stock-to-accounts agreement, and a tie-out difference traced to a delivery is investigated through this chapter's postings — the stock ledger row, the accounting entry, and the document, read together.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Returns
lessons.html:
Goods come back. This chapter is the return lane: the document, the condition decision, and the commercial tie.

1. The return Delivery Note. The return is recorded on a Delivery Note marked as a return (Is Return), created from the original Delivery Note so the rows, rates, and references carry:

1. The returned rows and quantities — what physically came back, counted at receipt against the customer's return advice.
2. The identity confirmed — batch and serial numbers on the returned rows checked against the original delivery's numbers: the business confirms it is receiving back what it shipped. A returned serial that was never delivered is a stopped line and an investigation.
3. The reason code — from the defined set (damaged in transit, fault, wrong item, customer cancelled, near-expiry per agreement): the quarterly returns read aggregates by these codes.
4. Submission posts the reverse movements — stock re-enters the receiving warehouse; the accounting reverses cost per the valuation rules; %delivered adjusts on the order.

2. The condition decision. Returned goods do not re-enter saleable stock automatically. At receipt, the condition decision routes the goods:

1. Saleable — undamaged, in date, sealed per the policy's saleability criteria: received into the trading warehouse.
2. Quarantine — damaged, suspect, opened, or requiring inspection: received into the quarantine warehouse (the Inventory track, module 1), and resolved from there through the inspection outcome — restored, written off through the damage lane, or returned to the supplier where the fault is upstream.
3. The pharmaceutical rule — returned pharmaceutical goods follow the compliance owner's saleability ruling; where regulation or policy prohibits resale of returned product classes, the quarantine-and-disposal route is the standing decision and the return's pricing reflects it.

3. The commercial tie. The return's money side is module 7's territory, summarised here for the flow: the credit note (the return Sales Invoice) issues against the returned quantities per the policy — full credit, replacement, or repair per the case — and the customer's balance and statement reflect it. The rule at the boundary: the stock document records what came back; the credit document records what the business owes for it — two documents, each stating its own event, linked.

4. The return window and authorisation. The policy states the return window per product class and the authorisation required: returns inside the window per the standard lane; returns beyond it as exceptions with named approval; returns of non-returnable classes refused with the policy reference. The authorisation is recorded on the return document, and the monthly returns read lists exceptions with their approvers.

5. Replacements. Where the resolution is replacement rather than credit: the replacement ships as a new Delivery Note against the order or against the replacement procedure the site uses, with its own verification and identity capture; the faulty unit's return and the replacement's despatch are two documents whose references link them. Warranty-covered replacements additionally update the serial record's warranty history (the Inventory track, module 3).

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The delivery reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the delivery function, each with its cadence and action.

1. The pending-acknowledgment read — weekly. Submitted Delivery Notes without an attached signed copy, by age. Each is chased to its proof of delivery; the file's completeness is the measure. An unacknowledged delivery is an unproven custody transfer, and the read keeps the exposure short.

2. The delivered-not-billed read — weekly. Module 4's read, operated from the delivery side: submitted deliveries whose invoicing has not followed within the cadence. The list feeds module 7's invoicing run and clears at each run.

3. The overdue and at-risk rows — weekly. Module 4's planning read continues through execution: rows past date, rows due with short stock — each with owner and action.

4. The returns read — monthly. The month's returns by reason code, customer, item class, and value:

1. The reason distribution — transit damage rising routes to the carrier and packing review; wrong-item returns route to the picking procedure; fault returns route to the supplier quality lane (the Procurement track).
2. The exception list — beyond-window and non-standard returns with their approvers.
3. The condition outcomes — returned value by route (saleable, quarantine, write-off): the figure that states what returns actually cost.

5. The transit-damage read — quarterly. Damage-coded returns and delivery discrepancies grouped by transporter and route, from the Delivery Note transporter fields. The output is data for the carrier review: rates per carrier per route, with the documents referenced. Findings route to the despatch procedure (packing), the carrier conversation (performance), or both.

6. The despatch verification sample — monthly. A sample of the month's Delivery Notes checked for the procedure's evidence: the verification step recorded, identity complete on controlled rows, acknowledgments attached, posting dates matching despatch dates. The sample is the procedure's audit; findings correct the procedure or the training, per the standing pattern, and the sample's results file with the month's read outputs.

7. The filing. The delivery file per order — Delivery Notes, acknowledgments, discrepancy notes, returns and their resolutions — accumulates on the order file module 4 opened, keeping the one-lookup standard: any delivery question answers from the order's file.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: Montaigne wave one
lessons.html:
This chapter executes the first wave of the module 4 order. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

The wave. Wave one of the Montaigne AH rollout covers the first five branches: each receives 1 terminal, 1 scanner, and 1 printer. The order's per-row dates place the wave in the current week; the equipment arrived from the supplier inside the lead time and sits at the fulfilling warehouse with serials captured at receipt (the Procurement and Inventory tracks' receiving discipline).

Step 1 — the pick lists (Chapter 3). The planning read presents the wave; despatch is planned as one vehicle serving the five branches on one route. Five pick lists issue — one per branch — each listing the three items with serial-capture requirements.

Step 2 — five Delivery Notes (Chapters 2, 4). Per the one-document-per-destination rule, five Delivery Notes create from the order — one per branch, each carrying: the branch's shipping address (module 1's address set, titled by Montaigne's own branch codes), the three rows with quantity 1 each, and the picked units' serial numbers recorded at pick. Rates carry from the order (the 4% terminal concession intact on the terminal rows — the Delivery Note does not renegotiate prices).

Step 3 — verification and despatch (Chapter 3). The staged sets are checked by the second person: fifteen units against fifteen document rows, serials against labels, addresses against the load plan. The five documents submit as the vehicle loads; the despatch packs travel; the transporter fields identify the carrier leg.

Step 4 — the postings (Chapter 5). Each submission posts its stock ledger entries at valuation (the equipment's landed cost from the receiving flow), cost of goods sold under perpetual inventory, and the reservation release for the delivered units. %delivered on the order advances to the wave's proportion; the delivery-portion milestone (the 40% schedule row) becomes billable for the delivered branches, and module 7's invoicing run will draw it.

Step 5 — acknowledgments (Chapter 3). Each branch signs its copy; the five scans attach. One branch's acknowledgment records a discrepancy: the printer carton shows transit damage. The discrepancy routes the same day.

Step 6 — the return lane runs (Chapter 6). The damaged printer returns on a return Delivery Note created from the branch's original document: one row, quantity 1, the unit's serial confirmed against the delivered serial, reason code damaged in transit. The condition decision routes the unit to quarantine; the inspection confirms the damage; the supplier-quality lane takes the unit (the fault is upstream). A replacement ships as a new Delivery Note with its own serial and acknowledgment, the two documents cross-referenced. The transit-damage read records the incident against the carrier and route.

The wave closes. Five deliveries acknowledged, one return resolved by replacement, the order file carrying the complete wave: five Delivery Notes, five acknowledgments, one return pair. Waves two and three remain on the order with their dates, and the planning read will present them in their weeks.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in delivery operations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the document that does not match the despatch. Symptom: quantities, warehouses, or identities on the Delivery Note differing from the physical load; both the customer's receipt and the stock records inheriting the difference. Correction: the discrepancy traced and corrected by the proper documents. Prevention: picking against the list, identity captured at pick, and the second-person verification before submission.

Error 2 — the unsubmitted despatch. Symptom: goods leaving with the Delivery Note still in draft; stock records showing goods the shelf no longer holds; custody transferred with no record. Correction: the document submitted with the honest despatch date and the gap noted. Prevention: submission at the moment of despatch as the standing procedure.

Error 3 — the missing acknowledgment. Symptom: deliveries without signed copies; delivery disputes with no proof; the file incomplete. Correction: acknowledgments chased through the weekly read. Prevention: the signed copy as part of the despatch procedure, and the pending-acknowledgment read.

Error 4 — the cancelled truth. Symptom: despatches that physically happened cancelled in the system to undo them; custody and cost misstated; the return lane bypassed. Correction: the cancellation reversed; the return documented as the physical event it was. Prevention: the correction-lane rule — cancellation only where goods did not leave; returns for goods that did.

Error 5 — returns straight to shelf. Symptom: returned goods re-entering saleable stock without the condition decision; damaged or non-resaleable product sold onward. Correction: the affected stock quarantined and inspected. Prevention: the condition decision at receipt, with the pharmaceutical saleability ruling applied.

Error 6 — the unread returns pattern. Symptom: returns processed individually with no aggregation; transit damage, picking errors, and supplier faults continuing because no read connects the cases. Correction: the returns and transit-damage reads compiled from the reason codes. Prevention: reason codes on every return and the monthly and quarterly reads.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the Delivery Note walk including addresses, honest dates, source warehouses, and identity on controlled rows; run picking, verification, despatch, and acknowledgment with their records; execute partial rows and waves under the one-document-per-destination rule and the tolerance settings; state the four postings of submission and the three correction lanes; process returns with the identity check, reason codes, the condition decision, and the commercial tie; and run the six delivery reads.

Module rule 5: the Delivery Note states what physically left — created from the order, identified at pick, verified by a second person, submitted at despatch, acknowledged at receipt, corrected only through the lane that matches what physically happened, and returned goods re-entering stock only through the condition decision. Module 6 covers taxes, pricing rules, and invoicing preparation.

taxes_invoicing.title: Selling 6 — Taxes, Pricing Rules & Invoicing
taxes_invoicing.desc: VAT done right, inclusive vs exclusive, item tax overrides, pricing rules and discounts, the Sales Invoice, payments, credit notes — and the reports that watch it all.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — VAT in Nigeria & the tax architecture
lessons.html:
Every naira of VAT you charge is money you are holding for the government. That single sentence reframes tax from paperwork into fiduciary machinery, and this chapter builds the machinery view a consultant needs before touching a single template.

Output VAT, in one paragraph. Nigerian VAT stands at 7.5%. When you sell taxable goods, you charge it ON TOP of your price (or embedded within it — Chapter 4); the amount is output VAT, and it is not revenue. It accrues into a VAT liability account, and each month the firm files and remits to FIRS — returns due by the 21st of the following month — netting output VAT collected against input VAT paid on purchases. Your firm is a collection agent with a deadline; the system's job is to make the collected number exact, automatic, and auditable.

The architecture principle: write once, apply everywhere. ZhiftERP encodes tax as a Sales Taxes and Charges Template — the policy object — selected on documents, never re-invented on them. One template row says: VAT, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output account. Every quotation, order and invoice that selects the template computes identically, and the liability account accumulates the truth as a by-product of trading. The rejected alternatives define the principle by contrast: VAT typed into item rates hides tax inside price (misstating both, unremittable as a number); VAT computed per document by hand varies with the human; VAT inferred from customer group confuses who is buying with what is taxable.

The account head. The template row names the ledger account the tax posts to — the VAT output liability in your chart. This is the joint where selling meets accounting: at month-end, the filing figure is READ from that account, and Chapter 9 shows the reconciliation that proves it against the invoice register. A template pointed at the wrong account (an income account, a random liability) files fiction with a straight face; verify the head once at setup and the joint holds forever.

Who decides what. Configuration is a consultant-plus-accountant conversation: the accountant owns which accounts and what the firm's filing posture is; the consultant owns encoding it so the sales floor never has to know. The seller's entire tax job, done right, is selecting the correct template — and Chapters 2-4 make even that mostly automatic.

The NGE thread. Where regulatory e-invoicing applies — the FIRS pipeline your NGE Portal serves — the invoice data transmitted downstream is only as clean as this architecture: the VAT the platform reports IS the template-computed figure on template-driven documents. A firm whose tax lives in templates passes e-invoicing validation as a by-product; a firm whose tax lives in typed rates and habits meets the mandate as a re-implementation project. Architecture first is also compliance first.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Building Sales Taxes and Charges Templates
lessons.html:
The template is a small machine: ordered rows, each computing a charge and posting it somewhere. Build one deliberately once and you will read every tax section in the system fluently forever.

Row anatomy. Each row carries: a Type — the computation base; the Account Head — where it posts; the Rate (or amount); and a description that prints. The types to command:

  • On Net Total — the workhorse: percentage of the document's net (pre-tax) total. Nigerian VAT is one row, On Net Total, 7.5%, VAT output account.
  • Actual — a fixed amount regardless of totals: a ₦15,000 delivery charge as a line the customer sees, posting to a freight-recovery account.
  • On Previous Row Amount / Total — compounding bases for cascading levies; rare in plain Nigerian trade but the reading knowledge matters — when you meet a template using them, the ORDER of rows is part of the arithmetic.

Charges are rows too. The same machinery carries non-tax charges — delivery fees, installation surcharges — each with its own account head. A document then presents goods, charges, and VAT as distinct lines summing to one grand total (Selling 3, Chapter 4 made the customer-facing case). Discipline: charges post to their own recovery accounts, never mingled into the VAT head — the filing figure must stay pure.

How many templates. Few. A standard-rated template (VAT 7.5%); perhaps a with-delivery variant; a zero-VAT template for the export/exempt document cases Chapter 3 does not cover row-wise. Template sprawl — one per customer, one per month — is policy chaos: when the rate changes or an account is remapped, every template is a separate edit and a separate chance to miss one. Encode DIFFERENCES that are item-level as Item Tax Templates (Chapter 3), not as document-template proliferation.

Defaulting. Mark the standard template as default and it lands on new documents automatically; the customer master and item defaults refine from there. The goal state: a rep raising an ordinary quotation never touches the tax section and it is still exactly right — because the right answer was configured, not remembered.

Change control. When FIRS moves the rate, the change is: edit the template row (with effective-date handling per accounting guidance), test on a draft, announce. One object, one edit, whole system consistent — the payoff of write-once, collected precisely when it matters most.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Item Tax Templates: exempt and zero-rated rows done right
lessons.html:
Not everything on a Nigerian invoice is standard-rated, and the professional handles mixed taxability on ONE document without breaking the arithmetic for anything else. The instrument is the Item Tax Template.

The mechanics. An Item Tax Template attaches to an ITEM (or item group) and overrides the document template's rate for that row only. The document says VAT 7.5%; the exempt item's template says VAT 0% for me; the invoice computes 7.5% on the taxable rows and 0% on that row — one document, mixed taxability, correct totals, correct liability. The rejected alternatives each break something: deleting the document's tax row zeroes EVERY row (the taxable lines now under-charge); splitting into two invoices doubles the paperwork to dodge a solved problem; faking it with a discount misstates price AND still books VAT the filing must then unwind.

Exempt vs zero-rated — the distinction that marks a professional. Both charge the customer 0% VAT; they differ on the seller's side of the ledger. Zero-rated supplies (classically exports, and specified categories) are within the VAT system at a rate of zero — the sale is a taxable supply, reported as such, with input-credit consequences the accountant cares about. Exempt supplies (Nigerian law lists basic food items, medical products and services, educational materials, among others) sit OUTSIDE the charge — no VAT charged, different reporting line, different input-credit posture. The seller's number is 0 either way; the FILING is not. Configuration follows the accountant's classification of each item class; the consultant's job is encoding that classification as item tax templates so documents get it right unattended — and knowing enough to ask the classification question rather than guessing.

Application discipline. Attach at the most stable level: an item GROUP template covers a whole exempt class (medical consumables) in one object; item-level templates handle the exceptions. Audit the mapping when the catalog grows: the new exempt item created without its template quietly charges 7.5% until a customer or an auditor notices — Chapter 9 meets that ticket, and the monthly cross-check (exempt-classified items vs items carrying the template) prevents it.

Reading a mixed invoice. The tax section shows the computed rows; per-line taxability is visible in the item tax detail. Teach clients to READ it once — the pharmacist who sees their exempt medicals at 0% and their taxable cosmetics at 7.5% on one clean invoice stops phoning about tax forever.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Inclusive vs exclusive: the arithmetic in full
lessons.html:
One checkbox separates two pricing worlds, and confusing them misstates either your price or your VAT return. This chapter makes the arithmetic reflexive in both directions.

Exclusive (the default). The entered rate is the NET price; tax adds on top. Rate ₦1,000, VAT 7.5% → tax ₦75, total ₦1,075. B2B trade lives here: procurement offices think in net prices and input credits, and your quotations (Selling 3) show net, VAT, gross as separate honest lines.

Inclusive. The tax row's inclusive setting means the entered rate already CONTAINS the tax. Rate ₦1,075 inclusive → net ₦1,000, VAT ₦75. The arithmetic, both directions, cold: net = inclusive ÷ 1.075; VAT = inclusive − net (equivalently inclusive × 7.5/107.5). Drill it: ₦2,150 inclusive → ₦2,000 net + ₦150 VAT. ₦10,750,000 inclusive → ₦10,000,000 net + ₦750,000 VAT. Retail-facing trade lives here: shelf prices are what-you-pay, and the system extracts the embedded VAT for the filing.

The two misconfiguration disasters, named. (1) Prices set as tax-inclusive but the row left EXCLUSIVE: the system adds 7.5% on top of a price that already contained it — the customer is overcharged (tax on tax), and the firm looks either greedy or incompetent at the till. (2) Prices set net but the row marked INCLUSIVE: the system carves VAT out of what was meant to be pure revenue — every sale silently yields 93.02% of its intended net, and the margin erosion hides until someone reconciles a month. Both diseases are one checkbox misaligned with one price-entry convention; the cure is a declared convention per price list (this list is inclusive; that one is net) and the checkbox matching it — checked once at setup, audited when lists are added.

One regime per document. Never mix conventions on a single document; per-list declaration keeps regimes segregated by construction, since documents inherit one list (Selling 2). Where a business genuinely runs both worlds — counter retail inclusive, B2B exclusive — that is two price lists and two document flows, each internally consistent, meeting only in the ledgers where both post exact VAT.

Presentation. Inclusive documents can still BREAK OUT the VAT in totals for the customer's paperwork (Selling 3, Chapter 4) — showing inclusive line prices and an extracted VAT figure is the honest retail-adjacent format, and it is what a VAT-registered buyer needs to claim their credit.

A worked till moment. The counter sells three items off the inclusive retail list — ₦2,150, ₦4,300, ₦1,075 shelf prices. The receipt totals ₦7,525; the totals section extracts ₦525 VAT (7,525 × 7.5/107.5) over a ₦7,000 net, and the day's VAT liability accrues to the naira without the cashier knowing the word regime. Meanwhile the B2B desk quotes the same goods off the exclusive list at their net rates plus a visible ₦525 VAT line. Same goods, same tax truth, two presentations — each native to its buyer.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Pricing Rules: anatomy & design
lessons.html:
A Pricing Rule is policy that fires itself: when conditions match, a discount or special rate applies — no memo, no memory, no rep discretion required. This chapter is the anatomy and the design doctrine.

The anatomy — three parts.

  • WHO and WHAT it applies to — conditions on the parties and goods: item, item group, or brand on one axis; customer, customer group, or territory on the other. The clean trees you built in Selling 1 and 2 are the targeting system: a rule aimed at group Distribution or territory South-West hits exactly what those trees define — mushy trees, mushy policy.
  • WHEN and HOW MUCH — quantity brackets (min/max qty: the 50-carton threshold), and validity dates (valid from/to: the Q4 window). Date-bounded rules start and STOP themselves — the promo that ends on schedule with no cleanup, the same self-executing elegance as validity-dated Item Prices (Selling 2, Chapter 6).
  • THE EFFECT — a discount percentage, a discount amount, or an outright special rate for the match.

So the running example assembles itself: 10% off, item group Beverages, customer group Distribution, min qty 50 cartons, valid 01-Oct to 31-Dec. Built once; fires on every qualifying order; dies on New Year's Day.

Priority and stacking. When several rules match one row, priority decides which applies — and rules can be set not to stack, so the winner applies alone. Design doctrine: engineer for ONE obvious winner per realistic scenario. A row where three overlapping rules fight, resolved by priority numbers nobody remembers, produces the Chapter 9 ticket — a surprising discount nobody can explain without a whiteboard. If you cannot state in one sentence which rule governs a given sale, the rule set is too clever.

Rules vs the other pricing instruments — the placement doctrine, complete. Base reality lives in price lists (Selling 2): who structurally pays what. Conditional policy lives in pricing rules: IF this buyer, this volume, this window. Genuine one-off negotiation lives in the document's Rate (Selling 3): visible, measured exceptions. Each instrument misused as another causes a known disease: rules patching stale base rates (Selling 2, Chapter 6's conviction), lists cloned per quarter to fake date-bounds, overrides doing structurally what a rule should. Place each policy at its level and every price on every document has one findable explanation.

Lifecycle. Rules are disabled when retired, never deleted while history references their period — the explanation of last Q4's pricing should remain readable next year. Few, legible, dated, owned: the four adjectives of a healthy rule set.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Discounts governance
lessons.html:
Discounts are where pricing policy meets human nature; governance is what keeps the meeting civilised. This chapter assembles the controls you have met into one posture.

The three instruments, at policy altitude. Selling 3 distinguished them mechanically; here is who should hold each. The row discount percentage / Rate edit — the negotiator's tool, for genuine per-deal concession, always visible against Price List Rate. The Additional Discount — a document-level cut on net or grand total: the whole-deal gesture (the MD shaving ₦200k off a ₦9.7m package to close), rare by nature, glaring by design — which is its virtue: nobody additional-discounts quietly. And pricing rules — policy discounts that fire themselves (Chapter 5), which is where anything RECURRING belongs.

The escalation ladder. A healthy shop runs concessions up a ladder: list price → rule-given discount (automatic, no approval needed — it IS the approval, pre-granted) → the rep's negotiated margin within a known band → beyond the band, escalation to the sales lead — and the floor under the whole ladder is Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate (Selling 8), the below-cost block that makes the worst outcome impossible at the keyboard. Where approval workflows are configured, the band is enforced by the system; where they are not, the band is enforced by the review — either way there IS a band, stated, known.

Measurement — the governance that actually governs. Because every concession is visible (Rate vs Price List Rate; additional discounts as fields; rules as named objects), discount behaviour is REPORTABLE: realised discount by rep, by customer, by item group, by period. The monthly read answers the questions that matter: who concedes most, to whom, and did the volume justify it? The pathological reading it catches early: the discount-everything culture — when average realised discount creeps up quarter on quarter, list prices have quietly stopped being prices, and the fix is Selling 2's repricing plus a re-anchored band, not another memo.

Free goods, restated as governance. The two-row treatment (100 at rate + 20 at zero, Selling 3) is a governance feature: free quantity is VISIBLE quantity — countable in stock (the 20 really left), attributable in reports (who gives away how much), and honest at the gate. Bundled free goods hidden in doctored rates fail all three at once.

The posture in one sentence. Structure in lists, policy in rules, exceptions on documents, a floor in configuration, and a monthly mirror in reporting — a firm holding that posture can negotiate hard all day without ever losing track of what its prices are.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The invoice bridge
lessons.html:
The Sales Invoice deserves — and has — its own full module: Selling 7 treats creation paths, statuses, Payment Entries, advances, write-offs and credit notes at manual depth. This chapter is the bridge: what THIS module's tax-and-pricing machinery hands to it, and the working vocabulary you need before crossing.

The accounting event, located. On the timeline law (Selling 5): order reserves, delivery deducts, invoice books, payment settles. Submitting the Sales Invoice books revenue and the customer's receivable — and, this module's addition: it also crystallises the VAT. The template you configured (Chapters 1-2), the item overrides (Chapter 3), the inclusive/exclusive regime (Chapter 4), the rule-given and negotiated discounts (Chapters 5-6) — all of them converge on the invoice, whose tax rows post to the liability account that the monthly filing reads. Everything upstream was policy; the invoice is where policy becomes a ledger fact FIRS can ask about.

Creation, one sentence each. From the order (billing ahead or alongside — the Montaigne advance) or from the DN (billing exactly what shipped) — the create-from spine unbroken; Selling 7 Chapter 1 gives the full treatment including the standalone and Update-Stock cases and their traps.

Status vocabulary, for reading lists today. Unpaid → Partly Paid → Paid; Overdue the moment the due date passes unpaid; Credit Note Issued when a return invoice stands against it. Enough to read any invoice list correctly; the collections craft built on it is Selling 7 Chapters 2-4.

Two handoffs to carry across the bridge. First, the To-Bill worklist: Selling 5 left delivered-unbilled DNs as a quiet alarm; the invoice is the answer, and Selling 7 formalises the oldest-first routine with an owner and a measured DN-to-invoice-days metric. Second, the credit note: Selling 5, Chapter 7 reversed stock on the return DN and named its money half — the Sales Invoice with Is Return, against the original — whose full mechanics (statuses, correction doctrine, the FIRS-grade audit pairing) are Selling 7 Chapter 4. Hold the pairing sentence until then: stock reverses on the return DN; money reverses on the credit note.

Why the split matters. Tax-and-pricing is POLICY work — configured by consultants, owned by accountants, invisible to good reps. Invoicing-and-collections is OPERATING work — daily, human, cash-critical. One module per altitude; the bridge is the invoice they share.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The three watching reports
lessons.html:
Configuration without reading is faith; this chapter is the reading. Three reports, one weekly habit, and the commercial review they feed. A sales professional who reads these weekly manages a book; one who does not, gets managed by it.

Sales Analytics — what is selling, to whom, where. Revenue cut by customer, item, item group, customer group, or territory, across time periods — every dimension you disciplined in Selling 1-2 now pays rent. The three reads to practice: trend (this quarter vs last, per cut — growth and its location); mix (which groups carry the number — the Services share your recurring-revenue story lives in); and the read that saves relationships: the quietly shrinking customer — an account down 30% across three periods announces churn a year before it resigns, and the response is a next step on the pipeline (your own cadence machinery), not a shrug at year-end. Group by customer, sort by decline, act on the top five: fifteen minutes that outperform most CRM dashboards.

Sales Order Analysis — the promise backlog. Ordered vs delivered vs billed across all open orders: the company's delivery backlog on one screen, readable by amount and by age. This report — not the DN list (Selling 5 taught why: DNs record what DID ship) — answers what stands promised and unperformed. The reads: overdue-to-promise rows (the delivery-date discipline of Selling 4 making lateness visible); the delivered-not-billed column (the To-Bill leak, quantified in naira); and per-customer slices for the account conversations. Warehouse planning, billing chase, and customer honesty all drink from this one well.

Accounts Receivable — who owes what, aged. Outstanding per customer, bucketed 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days. The professional read is right to left: the 90+ column first (each entry a story with a name — dispute? distress? neglect?), then 61-90 (this month's interventions, before they graduate rightward), then the near buckets (the healthy hum). Left-to-right reading — admiring the big healthy 0-30 — is the complacency read; the money that kills firms is always in the right-hand columns, aging politely. Every right-column entry gets an owner and a dated next step (Selling 7 builds the full collections craft on exactly this).

The cadence and the page. Weekly, thirty minutes, all three — and quarterly, ONE page for the commercial review: revenue trend and mix (Analytics), backlog and slippage (Order Analysis), ageing shape (AR), beside the pipeline and lost-reason reads from Selling 3. One page, five graphs, every number traceable to documents. Boards steer on it; the alternative is anecdote with a projector.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study & support patterns
lessons.html:
First the build, then the scar tissue — HealthTrade (Selling 2's dual-channel vendor) gets its full tax-and-pricing layer, and then the seven tickets this layer generates in the wild.

THE BUILD. Step 1 — the VAT spine (Ch. 1-2): one standard template — VAT, On Net Total, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output liability the accountant confirmed — set as default; a delivery-charge variant for the routes that bill freight, its Actual row posting to freight recovery, never the VAT head. Step 2 — the exempt class (Ch. 3): medical consumables are exempt per the accountant's classification — one Item Tax Template at the item-group level covers the whole class at 0%; cosmetics and equipment stay standard. A test invoice mixing both shows 7.5% and 0% rows computing side by side, and the pharmacist-facing print is clean. Step 3 — the regimes (Ch. 4): the counter retail list is declared INCLUSIVE (shelf prices are what-you-pay; the checkbox matches), B2B lists stay exclusive; the ₦2,150 shelf item books ₦2,000 net + ₦150 VAT without a human thinking. Step 4 — the Q4 rule (Ch. 5): 10% off, Beverages group, Distribution group, min 50 cartons, 01-Oct to 31-Dec — one object; it will die on schedule. Step 5 — the governance frame (Ch. 6): below-cost validation on; the negotiation band stated (reps to 5%, lead to 12%); the monthly discount read scheduled. Step 6 — first reads (Ch. 8): month one's Analytics shows the mix baseline; Order Analysis quantifies a ₦4.1m delivered-not-billed leak (fixed by Thursday); AR's right columns are, for now, empty — the goal is keeping them so.

THE PATTERNS. 1 — VAT found typed inside item rates: the pre-system habit imported (Ch. 1); prices misstated, liability unfiled as a number; fix by re-basing prices net (or declaring inclusive properly) and letting the template compute. 2 — a tax row deleted to exempt one item: every row on the document went to zero (Ch. 3); the taxable lines under-charged; fix with the Item Tax Template and re-issue. 3 — margins mysteriously 7% thin on one list: the inclusive checkbox on a net-priced list (Ch. 4, disaster two); realign convention and checkbox, reprice the damage window. 4 — a surprising discount nobody can explain: rule stacking with forgotten priorities (Ch. 5); fix by simplifying to one-obvious-winner and disabling the fossils. 5 — average realised discount creeping quarterly: the discount-everything culture (Ch. 6); the fix is repricing plus a re-anchored band — a commercial decision the report forced into daylight. 6 — the filing figure disagrees with the invoice register: something posted to the VAT head that was not document VAT, or a template mis-aimed (Ch. 1-2); reconcile the account to the register monthly so the 21st is never a surprise. 7 — the AR read as good news while 90+ grows: left-to-right complacency (Ch. 8); institute the right-to-left read with owners on every right-column name.

The fifth law. Selling 1-2: documents are downstream of masters. Selling 3: the pipeline is downstream of discipline. Selling 4: the order is the single source of fulfilment truth. Selling 5: the DN is where the word meets the world. This module: tax and price are POLICY — encode once, apply everywhere, and audit by report. A firm that holds this law negotiates freely, files calmly, and explains any number on any document in one sentence; a firm that does not, improvises both its prices and its taxes — and eventually explains itself to FIRS instead.
