sales_invoice.title: Selling 7 — The Sales Invoice, Payments & Collections
sales_invoice.desc: The accounting event in full: creating invoices from orders and delivery notes, what submission books, due dates and payment terms, Payment Entry mechanics including advances and allocation, credit notes, and the receivables discipline that turns sales into cash.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The invoice as the accounting event
lessons.html:
Everything in Selling 1-6 was preparation for this document. The Sales Invoice is where money becomes real on the books: submitting it books revenue and the customer's receivable into the general ledger, dated by its posting date, and — Selling 6's addition — crystallises the VAT to the liability account the monthly filing reads. Nothing else does this: the order promised, the DN moved goods, the payment (later) settles what the invoice creates. When any question begins when do the books recognise…, the answer is: at invoice submission.

The ledger effect, spelled out. One submission posts: debit the customer's receivable (they owe you the gross), credit revenue (the net), credit VAT output (the tax) — and, in perpetual-stock configurations, the cost-of-goods entries ride the stock movement's valuation. A Sales Professional does not journal these; the point is to KNOW they happen, so that every conversation with the accountant, the auditor, or FIRS starts from the same picture.

Creation paths, chosen by flow:

  • From the Sales Order — billing ahead of or alongside delivery: the advance and milestone flows (the Montaigne 50/40/10, Chapter 9). The order's billed-quantity ledger counts down; the To-Deliver status keeps the physical promise visible after finance is satisfied (Selling 4).
  • From the Delivery Note — billing exactly what shipped: partial-delivery trade's honest path. The invoice quantities ARE the shipped quantities; the DN advances from To Bill toward Completed.
  • Standalone — for genuinely document-less sales; rare and suspicious in disciplined B2B, because a standalone invoice counts against no order and closes no DN.

The Update Stock invoice — full treatment of the trap. An invoice with Update Stock ticked moves inventory itself, playing delivery note and invoice in one document. Its legitimate homes: counter sales and cash-and-carry, service jobs consuming materials, any flow that deliberately skips the DN. The trap, precisely: tick it on an invoice made FROM a Delivery Note and stock deducts TWICE — once at the DN, once at the invoice — and the stock report begins lying by exactly the doubled quantities. The rule: in the standard flow (order → DN → invoice), Update Stock stays OFF; where it is ON, there is no DN in that flow at all. Auditing a client's flows for this one checkbox has recovered entire phantom-stock mysteries.

Two dates, permanently distinct. The posting date is when the books record the sale; the due date is when the customer must pay. They are computed differently, serve different masters, and conflating them is the root of half of all ageing-report confusion. The due date's engineering is Chapter 2's entire subject.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Payment terms & due-date engineering
lessons.html:
The due date is not typed; it is ENGINEERED — from Payment Terms that were agreed before the invoice existed. This chapter is that engineering, because the collections craft of Chapter 8 is only as strong as the dates it enforces.

The Payment Terms Template. A named schedule of when portions of an invoice fall due: Net 30 (100% at 30 days from posting); 50% Advance, Balance Net 15; the Montaigne 50/40/10 (50% in advance, 40% on delivery, 10% on commissioning — a three-portion template). Each portion carries its share and its due rule (days after posting, day-of-following-month, etc.). Build the firm's real commercial offers as templates ONCE; the sales floor then selects agreements, never invents arithmetic.

The inheritance chain. Terms flow: customer master → sales order → invoice. Set Net-45 on MediPlus's master (Selling 1, Chapter 8) and every order inherits it, every invoice computes its due date from it, and nobody decides terms at billing time — which is the governance point: terms are AGREED at relationship or deal level, with whatever approval that took, and billing merely executes the agreement. An invoice whose terms were improvised at creation is an agreement nobody made.

Due-date computation. From posting date plus the template's rule, per portion. A ₦10m invoice on 50% Advance / Balance Net 30, posted 1 September: ₦5m due immediately, ₦5m due 1 October — TWO schedule rows on one invoice, and the ageing report (Chapter 8) ages each portion by its own due date. This is why multi-portion templates beat splitting into multiple invoices: one invoice, one document for the customer's records, a schedule the system enforces portion by portion.

Retention — the 10% that waits. Project and installation trade holds a retention: the final portion due on commissioning, sign-off, or a defects period. Model it as the template's last portion with its longer rule — the Montaigne 10% is exactly this — so the retained amount ages correctly as NOT-YET-DUE rather than polluting the overdue columns, and surfaces on schedule when its trigger date arrives. Retentions tracked in someone's memory are retentions never collected; the schedule row is the memory.

Credit days and the limit. Terms interact with the credit limit (Selling 1, Chapter 6): longer terms mean more exposure per naira of monthly sales — the ₦15m limit that fits Net-30 strangles the same customer on Net-60. When terms are renegotiated, the limit review rides along; the two numbers are one risk decision wearing two fields.

Discipline summary. Templates for every real offer; terms on masters and orders, never improvised on invoices; multi-portion schedules for staged deals; retention as the last portion. Do this, and Chapter 8's collections machine runs on dates a court would recognise.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Statuses & reading the invoice book
lessons.html:
The invoice list, read correctly, is the firm's cash cockpit. This chapter is the vocabulary and the worklists.

The status vocabulary, complete:

  • Draft — being prepared; no ledger effect yet.
  • Unpaid — submitted; the receivable stands; no money allocated.
  • Partly Paid — some allocation received; outstanding visible. A ₦2m receipt against ₦5m leaves exactly this — never Paid, and no longer merely Unpaid.
  • Paid — outstanding cleared to zero (allocations plus any write-off, Chapter 6).
  • Overdue — the due date (or a portion's due date) passed while an outstanding remains. Automatic, merciless, and the single most useful filter in the module.
  • Credit Note Issued — a return invoice stands against it (Chapter 7).
  • Return — the credit note itself carries this, marking it as the reversal side.
  • Cancelled — the document lifecycle exit; its ledger entries reversed by cancellation, its number retained in history.

The three worklists, from one list:

  • Overdue, oldest first — collections (Chapter 8 operationalises it). Every entry is money the firm has EARNED and not received; the sort order is the priority order.
  • Unpaid, due this week — the pre-emptive list: a polite reminder BEFORE the due date converts more invoices than a firm letter after it. Nigerian B2B pays the supplier who asks on time.
  • Draft older than a day — the leak inside the house: invoices prepared and never submitted book nothing, age nowhere, and hide from every report. Drafts are a workspace, not a warehouse.

The To-Bill handoff, formalised. Selling 5 left delivered-unbilled DNs as an alarm; here is the standing routine. The owner: a named person (in an 11-person firm, the accountant or ops lead — named, not implied). The cadence: daily or twice-weekly, the To-Bill DN list oldest first, each becoming an invoice FROM its DN or carrying a written reason it cannot yet. The metric: DN-to-invoice days — median days between delivery and invoice submission. World-class is same-day to two days; a creeping median is the earliest possible warning that revenue is leaking between the warehouse and finance, visible weeks before it shows as a cash problem. Measure it, post it, and the handoff gap that Chapter 10 meets as a disease never forms.

The account view. Per-customer, all invoices, all statuses, schedule rows visible: the screen for the terms conversation, the statement dispute, the credit-limit review. Selling 4 gave account owners the promises screen; this is its cash twin — together they are the whole relationship on two tabs.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Payment Entry I: receiving money
lessons.html:
Money arrives; the Payment Entry records it — and records it in a way the BANK STATEMENT will recognise, which is the standard this chapter holds throughout.

Creation. From the invoice: Create > Payment — party, references and amounts pre-fill, and the entry is born allocated. The fields that matter:

  • Mode of Payment — transfer, POS, cash, cheque. Not decoration: modes map to accounts and to reconciliation behaviour, and a firm that records mode honestly can answer how much cash did the counter take Tuesday without a drawer count.
  • Paid To (the bank account) — the actual account the money entered. THE reconciliation field: month-end bank rec is matching entries to statement lines, and entries pointing at the wrong bank are the archaeology.
  • Reference number and date — the transfer reference, the teller number, the cheque number. Sixty seconds at entry; hours saved per dispute.
  • Allocation rows — which invoices, how much each. The entry's heart, and Chapter 5's subject at depth.

Full payment. Allocation equals outstanding; the invoice flips to Paid. The base case, worth one sentence.

Partial payment. Allocate what came; the invoice stands Partly Paid, outstanding visible and aging by its due date. Repeat as receipts arrive — three payments against one invoice are three entries, each matching a real bank line. Resist the anti-pattern of holding receipts unrecorded until the customer finishes paying: cash in the bank unrecorded in the ledger is the reconciliation break you built yourself.

The bank-line law. One real-world receipt = one Payment Entry. A customer's single ₦12m transfer is ONE entry (however many invoices it settles — Chapter 5); three separate cheques are THREE entries even if they arrived in one envelope. Entries mirror bank lines; when they do, reconciliation is a matching game; when they do not — receipts merged for convenience, or one transfer split into fabricated entries — every month-end begins with an investigation.

Journals are not receipts. A bare journal entry crediting the customer records a number while orphaning everything the Payment Entry carries: no reference, no mode, no allocation to specific invoices, no place in payment reports. Journals have their accounting uses; recording customer receipts is not one of them, and Chapter 10 meets the ledger that thought otherwise.

Posting date honesty, again. The entry's date is when the money moved — the statement's date, not the recording afternoon's. The same chronology law as the DN (Selling 5): ledgers are believed exactly as far as their dates are true.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Payment Entry II: advances, allocation & multi-invoice
lessons.html:
Real receipts rarely match one invoice neatly. This chapter is the allocation craft — the difference between a receivables ledger that answers questions and one that generates them.

One payment, many invoices. The ₦12m transfer settling four invoices: ONE Payment Entry, four allocation rows splitting the amount across the references — each invoice's outstanding reduced by its share, each flipping to Paid or Partly Paid as its share dictates. Which invoices, in what order? The default craft: oldest first, unless the customer's remittance advice says otherwise — and when it says otherwise, FOLLOW the advice and keep it on file, because allocation against the customer's instruction is how two correct ledgers come to disagree, and Chapter 10's allocation-drift disease is born from exactly this shortcut.

The advance — money before any invoice. Your enterprise reality: 50% before work begins. The mechanics: a Payment Entry against the customer with no invoice reference — the amount sits as an advance (unallocated credit) on the customer's account, visible in their balance, reducing their net exposure, waiting. It is NOT parked in a drawer until an invoice exists (unrecorded cash), NOT a negative invoice, NOT a discount promised against future billing.

Allocation — the advance meets its invoice. When the invoice is raised, the advance is allocated to it — pulled into the invoice's settlement so the outstanding nets down. The Montaigne flow in miniature: ₦4.85m advance received (entry against customer); first invoice ₦4.85m raised from the order; allocation applied; invoice Paid; advance consumed. The failure mode this discipline prevents is expensive and common: the advance sits unallocated forever, the invoice is paid by a fresh receipt or chased as overdue, and the customer is functionally double-credited — or rightly furious at being dunned for money they sent months ago. Chapter 10 names it the unallocated-advance black hole; the prevention is a standing monthly read of unallocated credits per customer, each one matched to its invoice or explained.

Partial allocation and mixed entries. An advance may cover part of a larger invoice (allocate the advance, balance stays outstanding on schedule); one entry may combine allocation to old invoices AND an advance residue for future ones — the rows express it exactly. The ledger's job is to mirror the commercial reality however untidy; the craft is expressing untidiness precisely rather than rounding it into fiction.

Refunding an advance. The deal dies after the deposit: the advance is refunded by a payment OUT against the customer, consuming the credit — documented, referenced, mirrored in the bank. Never a quiet journal, never keep it against something future unless the customer has agreed in writing to exactly that.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Write-offs, deductions & Nigerian short-pay realities
lessons.html:
The amount that arrives is often not the amount invoiced — and in Nigerian B2B, the difference is frequently LAWFUL. This chapter is the taxonomy of short payments and the exact treatment of each; mishandling them is the fastest way to fill an ageing report with fictional debts.

Reality one: Withholding Tax (WHT) deducted at source. The big one. Qualifying Nigerian customers — companies, government — are REQUIRED to withhold tax from certain payments (services and contracts prominently; rates commonly 5% for corporate service arrangements, with other categories at other rates — the firm's accountant owns the exact schedule) and remit it to FIRS on your behalf. So Montaigne, invoiced ₦1,000,000 for services, lawfully pays ₦950,000 and remits ₦50,000 to FIRS against your tax identity, issuing (eventually) a WHT credit note/certificate — which is REAL MONEY to you: creditable against your company income tax.

The treatment, exactly: the Payment Entry records ₦950,000 received, allocates the FULL ₦1,000,000 to the invoice, and carries the ₦50,000 as a deduction row posting to a WHT receivable asset account. The invoice closes Paid (the customer's obligation to YOU is fully discharged — part in cash, part in tax paid on your behalf); the receivable ledger is clean; and the WHT receivable account accumulates the certificates-to-chase balance. The wrong treatments, each with its cost: leaving ₦50,000 outstanding forever (a fictional debt that poisons the ageing and eventually gets dunned — embarrassing both firms); writing it off (donating a tax credit); a credit note (there was no return and no error — the price was right). The certificate chase is then a standing discipline: the WHT receivable is only worth its paper, so certificates are requested, logged against their deductions, and handed to the accountant for the income-tax credit — a monthly list, owned, like everything else in this module.

Reality two: bank charges on the receipt. The transfer arrives ₦4,850 light because a bank took its fee in transit. Same instrument: full allocation to the invoice, a deduction row posting the charge to bank-charges expense. The invoice closes; the expense lands where expenses live.

Reality three: the genuine short-pay. ₦1,999,820 against ₦2m — rounding, a customer's payment-run quirk, no dispute intended. Within the firm's configured write-off limit, the Payment Entry writes off the ₦180 to the write-off account and closes the invoice honestly. Chasing ₦180 forever costs more than ₦180; carrying it as outstanding pollutes every report it touches. Above the limit, it is not a write-off — it is either a dispute (Chapter 8's process) or an agreed adjustment (Chapter 7's credit note); the limit exists precisely to keep those categories from blurring.

What is NEVER the treatment: editing the invoice total to match the receipt. The invoice is the record of what was agreed and billed; the Payment Entry's deduction machinery exists so that every difference between billed and banked is CLASSIFIED — tax, charge, write-off — and lands in its own account with its own trail. An invoice edited to meet its payment has destroyed the only evidence of the difference.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Credit notes & the correction doctrine
lessons.html:
Submitted invoices are never edited and never deleted — their immutability is what makes the ledger evidence. Reversal and correction happen through the credit note, and this chapter is its complete mechanics plus the doctrine around it.

The instrument. A credit note is a Sales Invoice with Is Return ticked, made against the original invoice, carrying negative amounts: revenue reversed, VAT reversed, the receivable reduced — each by exactly the credited quantities and values, each linked to what it reverses. The original's status flips to Credit Note Issued; the credit note itself carries Return. Two documents, permanently married in the record.

The two occasions:

  • Returned goods — the money half of Selling 5's pairing: stock came back on the return DN; the credit note gives the money back its mirror. Raise it against the original invoice for the returned quantities — partial returns get partial credit notes, the linkage keeping every remainder honest. The pairing sentence, final form: stock reverses on the return DN; money reverses on the credit note; one physical event, two ledgers, two linked documents.
  • Billing corrections — wrong rate, wrong quantity, wrong customer even. The doctrine: credit note against the wrong invoice, then re-invoice correctly. Both documents stand forever: every figure that ever hit the ledger PLUS the visible instrument that unwound it. This is precisely what auditors and FIRS expect to find; the alternative culture — journals quietly patching invoice errors, or administrative edits to submitted documents — is what turns a routine audit forensic, because a ledger that can be silently corrected is a ledger that proves nothing.

What the customer does with a credit. Two lawful endings: the credit is applied against other invoices (allocated like a payment — the customer's next settlement nets it off), or refunded (a payment out, referenced, banked — Chapter 5's refund mechanics). Which one is the customer's call within the commercial relationship; the system's job is that the credit exists as a first-class balance until one ending consumes it — never an off-ledger IOU, never we will remember at the next order.

Credit notes and the VAT return. The reversed VAT flows back through the liability account — the month's filing nets it automatically because the credit note is a document like any other (Selling 6's architecture paying off in reverse). A credit given outside the system, by discount-on-the-next-invoice handshake, misstates two months' VAT at once.

Governance. Credit notes are powerful — they erase receivables — so they carry the same visibility posture as discounts (Selling 6): a monthly read of credit notes by value, reason, and raiser. A firm whose credit-note report is boring is a firm whose billing is accurate; a spike is either a quality problem upstream (returns — route to operations) or a billing-discipline problem inside (corrections — route to training). Either way the report knew first.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The collections craft
lessons.html:
Selling ends when the money is in the bank; collections is the craft of the last mile. It is a SYSTEM — cadence, instruments, escalation — not a mood that strikes when cash feels tight. This chapter builds the system.

The posture. Collections begins before anything is late: terms agreed on the offer (Selling 3), enforced dates engineered (Chapter 2), invoices submitted same-day-as-delivery (Chapter 3's metric). A firm that bills promptly and reminds politely is PAID first in its customers' payment runs — Nigerian B2B triages suppliers by who is organised, and everything below is that organisation made visible.

The weekly engine, four gears:

  • Gear 1 — the pre-due reminder. Invoices due within 7 days get a courteous note with the invoice attached. Cost: minutes. Effect: your invoice is IN the payment run instead of after it.
  • Gear 2 — the statement. Monthly, every credit customer receives a Statement of Account: invoices, credits, payments, balance. Customers dispute what they see quarterly; they PAY what they see monthly — and the statement surfaces allocation disagreements (Chapter 5) while they are one month deep, not eight.
  • Gear 3 — the overdue ladder. AR read right-to-left (Selling 6, Chapter 8), each right-column entry worked up a stated ladder: reminder → call with a promise-to-pay recorded — and in this house a promise-to-pay IS a dated next step on the board, with an owner, that fires (your v3.75 reminder machinery doing collections duty) → escalation letter → commercial measures.
  • Gear 4 — the commercial measures. The credit machinery from Selling 1 and 4, now used: the credit limit blocks new exposure automatically as outstandings swell; open orders go on Hold (Selling 4, Chapter 5) pending payment — the polite sentence is we have paused the next delivery while the account catches up, and it collects better than any letter because it is not a threat, it is a system behaving predictably.

Disputes, quarantined. A genuinely disputed invoice (wrong goods claim, pricing disagreement) is FLAGGED and worked as a dispute — investigation, resolution by credit note or by evidence — and NOT dunned while flagged: dunning a dispute hardens it. But the flag has an owner and an age limit; disputes are a queue, not a parking lot, and the monthly read includes disputes older than 30 days by name.

The metrics that steer. Three numbers, monthly: DSO (days sales outstanding — the book's overall speed); ageing shape (the % beyond 60 days — the risk concentration); promise-kept rate (of recorded promises-to-pay, how many landed — which tells you whose word prices at par). Post them where the commercial team sees them; collections improves fastest when it is measured in public and worked in private.

The tone. Every instrument above is polite, predictable, and relentless — the three adjectives that collect. Anger is amateur; silence is expensive; the system is neither.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: the Montaigne billing, settled to zero
lessons.html:
The deal that began as a quotation in Selling 3, committed in Selling 4, and shipped its waves in Selling 5 now runs its money to zero — through an advance, staged invoices, a lawful WHT deduction, a credit note, and a retention. Every chapter clocks in.

The frame (Ch. 2). Order value ₦9.7m on the 50/40/10 template: ₦4.85m advance, ₦3.88m on delivery, ₦970k retention on commissioning. The schedule lives on the terms; the invoices will inherit it.

Step 1 — the advance (Ch. 5). Before wave one ships, Montaigne transfers ₦4.85m. Payment Entry against the customer, no invoice yet — reference captured, bank account exact — sitting as an unallocated advance. The advance invoice is then raised FROM the order for the 50% portion; the advance is allocated; invoice Paid; credit consumed. (The Selling 4 hold episode — the four-day stall in Montaigne's approval chain — happened exactly here, and released here.)

Step 2 — wave billing (Ch. 1, 3). As each delivery wave completes, its invoice is raised from the DNs — billing exactly what shipped, branch by branch; the To-Bill DNs clear within a day (the metric holds at same-day), and the order's billed ledger climbs alongside its delivered ledger. Update Stock stays OFF throughout — the DNs moved the stock; the invoices move only money.

Step 3 — the lawful short-pay (Ch. 6). The 40% invoice (₦3.88m, service-heavy) is settled by Montaigne at ₦3.686m — 5% WHT of ₦194k withheld at source. The Payment Entry: ₦3.686m received, FULL ₦3.88m allocated, ₦194k deduction to the WHT receivable. Invoice Paid; ageing clean; and the certificate chase begins — logged, owned, requested with the same politeness as everything else, because that paper is creditable tax.

Step 4 — the DOA credit (Ch. 7). Selling 5's damaged terminal (T-88214, quarantined; T-88519 shipped as replacement) resolves commercially as a like-for-like swap: the replacement was invoiced on its wave, so a credit note against that wave's invoice for one terminal reverses the double-billing — negative quantities, linked to the original, the wave invoice flipping to Credit Note Issued for that line's value. Montaigne elects to apply the credit against the retention invoice rather than take a refund — noted, and waiting.

Step 5 — the retention (Ch. 2, 8). Commissioning signs off in week 10; the retention portion falls due ON SCHEDULE — it aged as not-yet-due the whole time, polluting nothing. The ₦970k invoice is raised; the parked credit allocates against it; the balance arrives inside terms after one pre-due reminder (Gear 1 earning its keep).

Step 6 — zero (Ch. 3, 5). The account view reads: every invoice Paid, no unallocated credits, WHT receivable carrying its ₦194k awaiting certificate, order Completed-and-Closed at 11 sets (Selling 4's honest ending). One deal, five modules, and any colleague can reconstruct every naira of it from the documents alone — which is the entire point of the machine.

The ledger of the deal: ₦9.7m committed → ₦8.897m banked + ₦194k in tax paid on the firm's behalf + ₦609k credited for the swap-and-retention netting — and not one number lives in anyone's memory.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Support patterns & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The cash module's scar tissue — the most expensive tickets in the entire manual, because every disease here IS money. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — stock report wrong by exactly the recent sales. Update Stock ticked on DN-based invoices (Ch. 1): every sale deducted twice. Fix: untick and correct the movements; audit the flow for which document owns deduction. The one-checkbox phantom-stock generator.

Pattern 2 — receipts recorded as journal entries. The pre-system habit (Ch. 4): balances roughly right, but no references, no modes, no allocations — reconciliation impossible, payment reports empty, and specific invoices still showing outstanding while the account nets fine. Fix: re-book as Payment Entries against their invoices; retire the habit with training, not memos.

Pattern 3 — the unallocated-advance black hole. Advances taken, never allocated (Ch. 5): customers dunned for invoices their deposits already covered, or double-credited when fresh receipts settle what the advance should have. Fix: the monthly unallocated-credits read, each matched to its invoice or explained; apologise to whoever got dunned — they were right.

Pattern 4 — the ageing full of fictional WHT debts. Lawful withholdings left as outstanding balances (Ch. 6): the 5% tails of every service invoice aging into the 90+ column, poisoning DSO, and eventually dunned — embarrassing the firm to its best corporate customers. Fix: re-book each with the deduction treatment to the WHT receivable; institute the certificate chase; teach the taxonomy of short-pays so cash application classifies instead of parks.

Pattern 5 — a submitted invoice was edited to match its payment. The evidence-destruction culture (Ch. 6, 7): the difference between billed and banked is now unexplainable forever. Fix: revert; classify the difference properly (deduction, write-off, or credit note); close the administrative permission that allowed it — and as with Selling 4's Pattern 7, this escalates as governance, because a quietly editable ledger proves nothing.

Pattern 6 — credit note raised with no return DN (or the reverse). The pairing broken (Ch. 7; Selling 5): money reversed while stock did not come back, or goods returned while the customer still owes the price. Each half-event leaves one ledger lying. Fix: complete the pair — the missing document, linked to its original — and reconcile the gap period.

Pattern 7 — allocation drift. Payments allocated by convenience against the customer's remittance advice (Ch. 5): both ledgers correct in total, disagreeing per invoice; every statement triggers a dispute about WHICH invoices are open. Fix: reallocate to match the advices on file; adopt the follow-the-advice rule; send statements monthly so drift surfaces at one month deep.

The sixth law. Selling 1-2: documents are downstream of masters. Selling 3: the pipeline is downstream of discipline. Selling 4: the order is the single source of fulfilment truth. Selling 5: the DN is where the word meets the world. Selling 6: tax and price are policy. This module: the invoice ledger is the cash truth, and collections is a system, not a mood. Every naira billed is classified on arrival — cash, tax withheld, charge, write-off, credit — every date is real, every promise has an owner, and the firm that holds this law is paid first, files calmly, and never argues with its own books.

Due date is the delivery date

A journal to patch the ledger

advanced.title: Selling 8 — Advanced Selling: Settings, Bundles, Blanket Orders & Sales Teams
advanced.desc: The advanced layer: Selling Settings in depth, Product Bundles, Blanket Orders for long-term rate agreements, and the two sales-team structures — Sales Person (internal, contribution and targets) and Sales Partner (external channel and commission).

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Selling Settings I: identity & defaults
lessons.html:
Selling Settings is where selling policy becomes system behaviour, and this module opens with its full treatment because everything advanced stands on it. Two chapters: identity and defaults here; the discipline switches next. A consultant should be able to defend every switch on this screen to a client's managing director — this pair of chapters is that defence, rehearsed.

Customer Naming By — the day-one identity decision. Customer Name makes the typed name the record's permanent ID (Alpha Pharmacy Ltd is both label and key); Naming Series issues CUST-00042-style IDs with the name as display. The decision rule, in full: portfolios with duplicate or near-duplicate names need the series. Nigerian trade is dense with them — an Adepoju Stores in three cities, a De Divine Pharmacy twice in one LGA, chains whose branches trade under near-identical registrations. Name-keyed records collide, and the workarounds (Alpha Pharmacy 2; Alpha Pharmacy - Ikeja one) are corruption of the identity layer itself. Series-keyed records are unambiguous forever while the display name stays human.

Why it is a DAY-ONE decision. The record's ID threads through every document, link and report that ever references it. Switching schemes after transactions exist is not a settings change — it is a data-migration project (re-keying, re-linking, testing), the kind of surgery your team performs for clients who decided casually and lived with collisions for two years first. The consultant's job at implementation is to ask the portfolio question — how many customers, how similar their names, how fast the growth — and decide ONCE, in writing, in the configuration workbook.

The defaults trio. Default Customer Group, default Territory, default Selling Price List: what new records and documents pre-fill with when nobody chooses. The doctrine from Selling 1-2, restated as configuration: point each at the genuinely commonest LEAF — never the tree root, never a Misc landfill — so hurried entry lands correctly; then pair the safety net with the weekly new-record review that catches what fell into it. Defaults are the difference between lazy data entry producing usable records and producing archaeology.

The reflex this pair of chapters builds. When a client asks can the system make our people do X or stop them doing Y, open this screen before answering anything. Most selling-policy questions are already switches; the expensive consultant is the one who scopes a customisation for a checkbox — and the credible one is the one who can also say which questions this screen does NOT answer, which is what the rest of this module maps.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Selling Settings II: the discipline switches
lessons.html:
Four switches carry most of the policy weight, and each maps to a question clients actually ask. Learn them as question-and-switch pairs.

Can we stop staff typing special prices? → untick Allow User to Edit Price List Rate. With it off, rates come ONLY from Item Price records — the rate field is read-only on documents for restricted roles. This is the strongest anti-discount control in existence: stronger than memos (forgotten), smaller price lists (worked around), or threats (negotiated). Pair it with the Selling 2 consequence: prices then move through exactly one door — the owned import workflow — and the firm can answer who changed what, when, from what to what, in one minute. The nuance a consultant adds: negotiation does not die; it moves to where Selling 6's governance ladder wants it — pricing rules for policy, escalation for exceptions — and the switch is often applied per role, leaving leads a band while the floor holds firm.

Can we prevent selling below cost? → Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate. The below-cost block at the keyboard: a rate under the item's purchase cost refuses at entry. Margin protection where it is cheapest — before the document exists — rather than where it is customary — in a month-end report after the goods have shipped. Its honest limitation, stated to clients: it guards against the accidental and the casual, not the determined (who escalates properly through the ladder), and cost accuracy upstream is its fuel — garbage purchase rates make it a random number generator, which is a data-hygiene conversation, not a reason to leave the floor open.

Can the agreed rate change between order and invoice? → Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle, plus its ACTION. The switch enforces that the Sales Order's rate cannot silently differ on the Delivery Note or Sales Invoice made from it — the drift the customer experiences as betrayal (₦850 signed, ₦880 billed). Its companion action setting chooses the response to a detected drift: Stop (hard block — strict shops, fixed-price trade) or Warning (allow but flag — shops with legitimate mid-cycle repricing, who then own their flags). Neither silence nor auto-correction is on the menu; the consultant's question to the client is simply which failure they prefer to be expensive: a blocked document at a busy moment, or a flagged drift someone must review.

Same item twice on one order? → Allow Item to be Added Multiple Times. The free-goods enabler (Selling 3's two-row treatment) and the two-rates-one-document case. It lives HERE — the address is itself an exam-grade fact.

And the global over-delivery allowance — the fallback under Selling 4's per-item tolerance: the house default for item classes that never got a specific number. Set it low; let bulk classes override upward deliberately.

The change-control coda. These switches move BEHAVIOUR, so they change like policy, not like preferences: decided with the client's management, dated, announced to the floor, never toggled casually mid-quarter to ease one loud complaint — Chapter 9 meets the shop where the edit-rate hole was quietly reopened for a friend, and what it cost.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Product Bundles I: construction & mechanics
lessons.html:
You price as ONE thing but pick as MANY things: the Pharmacy Starter Pack at ₦450,000 that is really shelving, a scanner, and a printer. The Product Bundle is the correct model, and this chapter builds one and traces it through every document.

The construction, in order:

  • The parent item. A normal item record BUT non-stock: Maintain Stock UNTICKED. The parent never has warehouse quantity — it is a commercial identity, not a physical one. Is Sales Item ticked (it must appear on selling documents); item group per the tree (a Bundles or Kits leaf keeps mix reporting honest); description written for the buyer, since it IS the one line they will read.
  • The bundle definition. The Product Bundle record: the parent on top, the child items with quantities beneath — 4 × shelf unit, 1 × scanner, 1 × printer. The children are ordinary stock items with ordinary bins.
  • The price. An Item Price for the PARENT on the selling list: ₦450,000 (Selling 2's machinery, one atom). Children need no selling price for the bundle to function — their prices, if any, serve their standalone sales.

The mechanics at each document — the part to recite: on the quotation, the order, and the invoice, the customer sees ONE line at the parent's price — clean commercial presentation, no per-child price exposure, no arithmetic for procurement to pick at. On the Delivery Note, the bundle EXPLODES: the packed-items section lists the children with their quantities, and it is the CHILDREN that move stock — 4 shelves, 1 scanner, 1 printer deducted from their bins; the parent deducts nothing, having nothing. Price lives on the parent; picking lives on the children. Serial-tracked children (the scanner) demand their serials on the packed rows exactly as Selling 5 taught — bundling changes presentation, never identity discipline.

Availability. A bundle is sellable as far as its SCARCEST child allows: 40 shelves, 3 scanners, 20 printers in stock means 3 packs, not 10 — the scanner is the binding constraint. Reading bundle availability is reading child bins with the definition in hand, and stocking for a bundle promotion means stocking its constraint (Chapter 4 operationalises this).

The rejected workaround, convicted once more. A stock-tracked starter-pack item with quantity of its own is a shelf lie: nobody counts packs, the children's bins and the pack's bin double-represent the same physical goods, and every stocktake becomes a reconciliation between fictions. The whole point of the bundle object is one physical truth (children in bins) wearing one commercial face (the parent's line and price).

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Product Bundles II: design & operations
lessons.html:
Chapter 3 built the object; this chapter is the judgment around it — when a bundle is the right model, what its margin really is, and how it behaves under operational stress.

Bundle vs variant vs separate lines — the placement test. Three lookalikes, three different objects. A variant (Selling 2, Chapter 3) is ONE product in versions — the polo in five sizes: one template, size children, each a stock item. A bundle is SEVERAL products sold as one line — priced together, picked separately. And sometimes the honest answer is separate lines on the quotation — when the customer negotiates the components individually, itemised billing serves the relationship better than a sealed price. The test in one sentence: variants VARY one thing; bundles COMBINE many things; and when the combination is negotiable per component, do not seal it.

Bundle margin — the arithmetic nobody does until it hurts. The parent has a price; the COST is the sum of the children's costs. Margin on the ₦450,000 pack = 450,000 minus (4 × shelf cost + scanner cost + printer cost) — and it MOVES whenever any child's cost moves, silently, because no single item record shows it. The discipline: bundles get a margin review on the same cadence as price lists (Selling 2's repricing rhythm), and Validate-Against-Purchase-Rate (Chapter 2) does not fully guard them — the parent, being non-stock, has no purchase rate of its own — so the bundle margin file is a deliberate, owned artefact. Bundles are where firms most often discover they have been selling below cost for a quarter, precisely because the loss hides in the sum.

Stock planning for the constraint. Availability equals the scarcest child (Chapter 3), so a bundle promotion is a procurement event for its binding constraint: launching 50 packs means the scanner order lands FIRST, and the reorder levels on children carry the bundle's demand, not just their standalone runs. The operational tell of unplanned bundles: shelves of three children and a stockout on the fourth, with sales blocked by the cheapest component.

Returns of bundles. The customer returns a pack — or one child of it. The stock half follows Selling 5 exactly: the return DN reverses the CHILDREN (all of them for a full pack; the specific child for a partial — the scanner back to quarantine by serial), because children are what moved. The money half follows Selling 7: the credit note against the invoice's parent line — full for a full return; for a partial, the commercial decision (proportional credit, or replacement of the child) is made explicitly and papered, because the parent's sealed price has no official per-child split. Mature firms keep an internal component-value split for the parent precisely to make partial-return credits non-arbitrary — another owned artefact of running bundles seriously.

Where bundles shine. Hampers and seasonal packs, starter and installation kits, promo combinations — anywhere the offer is genuinely one decision for the buyer. Model it once, correctly, and the bundle is a pricing weapon; model it as a fake stock item and it is a stocktake dispute with a marketing name.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Blanket Orders: the consumed agreement
lessons.html:
A customer commits to 10,000 cartons over six months at ₦820. More than an enquiry, less than a truck-now order: it is an AGREEMENT TO BE CONSUMED, and the Blanket Order is its instrument. This chapter is its complete lifecycle.

Creation. The blanket order carries the customer, the items with agreed quantities and agreed rates, and the from/to dates of the agreement. Submitting it creates NO reservation and moves NO stock — deliberately: the commitment is commercial, not logistical, and the warehouse plans from the drawn orders, not the frame. (Contrast Selling 4: a Sales Order reserves because it is a delivery promise; the blanket promises a RELATIONSHIP of deliveries.)

Drawing against it. Each real purchase is an ordinary Sales Order referencing the blanket, and two things happen by construction: the row inherits the agreed ₦820 — nobody renegotiates, nobody forgets the deal rate, no override fingerprints needed because the rate is the agreement's — and the blanket records the drawdown: ordered-so-far against committed. From the draw onward, everything is Selling 4-5-7 as normal: the order reserves, its DNs deduct, its invoices bill at the inherited rate.

Monitoring the consumption. The remaining commitment is read from the blanket order itself — ordered-vs-committed — and reviewing it monthly is account management with teeth: a customer at 20% drawdown four months into six is not going to make 10,000, and that conversation (extend? revise? let it lapse?) happens NOW, commercially, rather than as a surprise at expiry. Conversely a customer at 90% in month three earns the next-tier conversation early. The blanket turns volume promises from toasts into numbers.

Expiry and renewal. The to-date ends the agreement: draws after it do not inherit, and the lapsed blanket stands in history as the record of what was promised and what was actually taken — the single most honest input to the NEXT negotiation (last agreement: committed 10,000, drew 7,400). Renewal is a NEW blanket at newly agreed numbers; extending old paper to house a new deal muddies both, the same law as reopened orders (Selling 4) and resurrected quotations (Selling 3).

The instrument comparison, final form. One giant Sales Order for 10,000: reserves half a warehouse for months and lies about delivery intent. A six-month-validity quotation: an offer awaiting an answer impersonating an agreement being consumed — wrong semantics, no drawdown, no rate enforcement on draws. A pricing rule at ₦820: gives the rate but tracks no commitment and expires without a record of performance. The blanket is the only instrument that is simultaneously a rate lock, a volume ledger, and a renewal brief — which is why your Montaigne-class volume relationships belong on it.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Sales Person: the internal team
lessons.html:
Sales Person models your own force — and models it as a tree, because organisations report upward: Sales Director → Regional Managers → Field Reps. Results roll up the hierarchy automatically; the Lagos number is its reps' sum, the company number is the regions' — no spreadsheet ever built, no argument about whose figure is whose, because the figure is computed from the same documents that raised the invoices.

Designing the tree. The same three rules as every tree in this manual (Selling 1-2): one question (WHO on our side owns this revenue), mirror how management actually reviews (if the MD reviews by region, regions are the branches), and leaves assignable in two seconds (every rep is exactly one node). And the law Selling 1 Chapter 3 established from the other side: people live in THIS tree so that geography can live in Territory — when Tunde resigns, his node is deactivated and his accounts reassigned, while Ikeja remains exactly where it was. Trees that outlive their staff are the point.

Assignment and contribution. Selling documents carry a Sales Team section: one or MORE sales persons, each with a contribution %, summing to 100. The solo case is one row at 100. The worked deal splits honestly — 60/40 for the rep who ran it and the colleague who closed the technical objections — and reports credit each with their contributed share of the revenue, never double-counting the deal. The alternatives are all worse: two invoices for one sale (fragments the customer's paper), remarks (no report reads them), or the quiet convention that whoever types the order gets the credit (which is how CRM data becomes politics).

Targets. Each sales person carries targets by item group and period — ₦30m of Pharma for Q4 — and actuals accrue from their assigned transactions. Targets aimed through the item-group tree make product-mix strategy personal: the rep whose target is weighted toward Services sells Services. The governance fact that makes targets real rather than theatre: assignment precedes measurement — a target against transactions nobody assigned is a number floating over a void, and Chapter 9 meets target theatre in the wild.

The report. The Sales Person-wise Transaction Summary: each person's transactions, contributed amounts, performance against target — the league table, the commission basis, and the substance of the performance conversation. The honest consultant's sentence, verbatim, for every client who asks for sales-by-rep: only if sales persons are assigned on the transactions — the report is arithmetic over assignments; the discipline precedes the dashboard. Make the Sales Team section expected in the client's process (mandatory where their policy warrants), and the question answers itself weekly forever.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Sales Partner: the external channel
lessons.html:
A Sales Partner is a business OUTSIDE your company that brings you deals — a reseller, a referral agent, a channel distributor, an implementation firm that sources clients. The record carries the partner's identity, type, and the operative field: a commission rate. This chapter is the channel run properly.

On transactions. Select the partner on a Sales Order or Sales Invoice and two things happen: the deal is stamped as that channel's business — channel revenue becomes a reportable dimension like any other — and the document computes the total commission at the partner's rate: the liability you owe for the introduction, calculated per deal, automatically, at the rate the record holds rather than the rate anyone remembers.

The distinction to keep razor-sharp: Person vs Partner. Sales Person is internal — your staff, a tree, contribution percentages summing to 100, targets, performance management. Sales Partner is external — another business, a flat entity, a commission percentage, a payable relationship. They are not two names for one idea; commission is not the divider (both structures can drive earnings); and a partner is not a customer (they bring buyers; they are not the buyer). One transaction can lawfully carry BOTH: your rep (Sales Person, 100%) worked the deal a referral firm (Sales Partner, 5%) introduced — the rep is measured, the partner is owed, and neither fact crowds the other.

Paying the channel. Commissions settle from the Sales Partner-wise Transaction Summary — the system's own totals of each partner's stamped business and accrued commission. The rule with money attached: pay partners from the report, never from their claims. When the partner's invoice says ₦2.4m and your summary says ₦2.1m, the summary — built from the actual stamped transactions — is the negotiating position, and the gap is almost always deals the partner counts that were never stamped (a stamping-discipline conversation) or rates remembered differently (the record settles it). Channel programs die two deaths — over-payment and under-tracking — and the report prevents both.

Channel governance. Three habits make a partner program an asset: stamp at entry (the partner goes on the order when the deal arrives, not reconstructed at commission time); review quarterly (each partner's volume, commission, and — using Selling 3's lost-reason lens — the quality of what they bring); and paper the terms (rate, scope, exclusivities in the partner agreement, with the record's rate matching the paper). A channel run on these three is scalable revenue; run on WhatsApp and goodwill, it is a dispute subscription.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: the advanced layer, end to end
lessons.html:
One firm — recognisably shaped like a Nigerian retail-systems vendor — hardens its advanced layer in a single quarter. Every chapter clocks in; this is the module executed as a project.

The starting state. Growing customer file with name collisions beginning; rates editable by everyone; a starter pack modelled as a fake stock item nobody counts; a big distributor buying on remembered handshake rates; sales-by-rep answered by anecdote; one referral firm paid whatever it invoices.

Step 1 — identity & switches (Ch. 1-2). Customer Naming By moves to series — decided in writing before the file doubles again; defaults pointed at real leaves. The discipline set: edit-rate OFF for the floor (leads keep a band), validate-against-purchase ON, same-rate action set to Stop (fixed-price trade), the global over-delivery fallback at 2% with serialized classes at zero. Announced, dated, owned — and the first week's blocked below-cost quote is celebrated in standup, not resented: the floor held.

Step 2 — the pack done right (Ch. 3-4). The fake stock item is retired; a proper bundle replaces it: non-stock parent Retail Starter Pack at ₦450,000, definition of 4 shelves + scanner + printer, parent priced on the standard list. The margin file is built (current children's costs sum to ₦361,000 — 19.8% margin, reviewed monthly); the scanner is identified as the availability constraint and its reorder level raised before the promo. First sale: one clean line on the invoice, three children exploding on the DN, the scanner's serial captured. A month later a damaged printer comes back: child returned by the Selling 5 mechanics, proportional credit issued from the internal component split — non-arbitrary because the split existed.

Step 3 — the handshake becomes a blanket (Ch. 5). The distributor's ₦820-whenever-we-order is papered as a blanket order: 10,000 cartons, six months, the rate on the agreement. Draws inherit ₦820 untouched; month-two review shows 31% drawdown — on pace, noted. The account conversation now has a number instead of a vibe, and next renewal will negotiate from recorded performance.

Step 4 — the team tree (Ch. 6). Sales Person tree: Director → Lagos / South-West → five reps. Sales Team made expected on orders; the first split deal books 60/40 and both reps see their contributed revenue in the summary. Q4 targets set by item group — the Services-weighted target for the rep carrying the support-plan push. The dashboard the MD wanted for a year exists in week one, because assignment finally does.

Step 5 — the channel papered (Ch. 7). The referral firm gets a Sales Partner record at the agreed 5%, terms papered, stamping-at-entry instituted. Quarter-end: the partner invoices ₦2.4m; the summary says ₦2.1m; the gap is two deals never stamped (fixed forward) — paid ₦2.1m plus the corrected stamps, relationship intact BECAUSE the number had a source.

Quarter-end reads. Settings holding (zero below-cost incidents, three Stop events all legitimate); bundle margin drifted to 18.1% on a shelf-cost rise — repriced; blanket at 64% with six weeks left — extension conversation opened early; team summary driving the first data-based commission run; channel report reconciled in one meeting. The advanced layer, installed once, now runs itself — which is the entire point of Chapter 9's law.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Support patterns & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The advanced layer's scar tissue — and the close of the manual. Symptom → disease → fix, then the law that seals the track.

Pattern 1 — special prices are back. The edit-rate hole quietly reopened (Ch. 2) — usually for one loud friend-of-the-house, then for everyone. Fix: close it, route the friend through the ladder (a rule or an escalated band), and log settings changes as policy events with dates and owners; a discipline switch toggled casually is policy repealed silently.

Pattern 2 — the bundle parent has stock. Someone ticked Maintain Stock on the parent, or receipts were booked against it (Ch. 3): now packs and children double-represent the same shelves and the stocktake disputes itself. Fix: zero and untick the parent through proper stock documents, recount the children, and re-teach the one-physical-truth principle.

Pattern 3 — bundle sold below cost for a quarter. The silent-margin disease (Ch. 4): a child's cost rose; the parent's sealed price did not. Fix: the margin file with its monthly review — the loss was invisible precisely because no single record showed it.

Pattern 4 — blanket exists; orders ignore it. Draws entered as plain orders at ad-hoc rates (Ch. 5): the agreement neither enforces its rate nor records its drawdown — the worst of both worlds, paper without teeth. Fix: re-reference the draws, correct rate history where the customer was overcharged against the agreement, and make blanket-reference part of the order discipline for agreement customers.

Pattern 5 — the tree is a graveyard. Departed reps still active, their accounts orphaned, the rollup lying (Ch. 6). Fix: deactivate leavers, reassign their books the same week they exit — the tree review joins the offboarding checklist, because trees outlive staff only if someone prunes.

Pattern 6 — target theatre. Ambitious targets, empty summaries (Ch. 6): assignment never became process, so the numbers float over a void and the review meeting reviews nothing. Fix: assignment-precedes-measurement, made structural — the Sales Team section expected on every order, checked in the weekly hygiene pass.

Pattern 7 — the partner's invoice is the ledger. Commissions paid from claims because stamping lapsed (Ch. 7): over-payment or under-tracking, discovered whenever the relationship sours. Fix: reconstruct the quarter from transactions once, painfully; then stamp-at-entry and pay-from-the-report forever.

The seventh law — and the manual's close. Selling 1-2: documents are downstream of masters. Selling 3: the pipeline is downstream of discipline. Selling 4: the order is the single source of fulfilment truth. Selling 5: the DN is where the word meets the world. Selling 6: tax and price are policy. Selling 7: the invoice ledger is the cash truth. And this module: the advanced layer is structure that outlives staff — settings, bundles, blankets, trees and channels encode the firm's selling judgment so that it survives resignations, promotions, and busy Fridays. A ZhiftERP Sales Professional is, finally, someone who installs judgment as structure: who makes the right thing the default thing, the visible thing, and the measured thing — and then lets the system be as relentless as no human can be. That is the certification. Go and sit the exam.

questions.q: A retail chain has many branches with similar names. Customer Naming By should be:
questions.why: Series naming avoids collisions and keeps records unambiguous.

questions.q: The strongest control to stop staff typing "special prices" on documents is:
opts: Unticking Allow User to Edit Price List Rate
questions.why: Rates then come only from Item Price records.

questions.q: Blocking sales below cost at the point of entry uses:
opts: Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate
questions.why: The validation setting is margin protection built into entry.

questions.q: Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle can be configured to respond to a drift with:
opts: A Stop or a Warning, per the action setting
questions.why: The companion action setting chooses hard block vs warning.

questions.q: A Product Bundle's parent item must be:
questions.why: The parent is never counted in the warehouse; only children are.

questions.q: On a bundle sale, warehouse stock is deducted for:
opts: The packed child items on the Delivery Note
questions.why: The DN explodes the bundle; children move stock.

questions.q: The customer's invoice for a bundle shows:
opts: One line at the parent's price
questions.why: Price lives on the parent; picking lives on the children.

questions.q: A customer commits to 10,000 cartons over six months at an agreed rate. Model it as:
opts: A Blanket Order drawn down by individual Sales Orders
questions.why: Blanket orders are consumed agreements; quotations are offers.

questions.q: A Sales Order drawn against a blanket order inherits:
opts: The agreed rate, while the blanket tracks drawdown
questions.why: Rate flows from the agreement; drawdown is tracked against commitment.

questions.q: How much of a blanket commitment remains is read from:
questions.why: The blanket order itself tracks its consumption.

questions.q: Two reps split a deal 60/40. This is recorded via:
opts: Sales Team rows with contribution percentages summing to 100
questions.why: Contribution % splits credit without double-counting revenue.

questions.q: Sales Person is structured as:
opts: A tree so results roll up the hierarchy
questions.why: The tree gives regional and directorial roll-ups.

questions.q: "Show me sales by rep" only works if:
opts: Sales persons are assigned on the transactions
questions.why: The discipline of assignment precedes the report.

questions.q: Sales Person vs Sales Partner — the distinction is:
opts: Person is internal staff with contribution %; Partner is an external business with commission %
questions.why: Internal tree vs external channel — a document can carry both.

questions.q: Commission owed to a reseller is paid from:
questions.why: Pay channels from the system's totals, not their invoices' claims.

questions.q: Switching Customer Naming schemes after transactions exist is:
opts: A data-migration project — re-keying and re-linking, which is why it is a day-one decision
questions.why: Decide once, in writing, in the configuration workbook.

questions.q: Defaults (group, territory, price list) should point at:
opts: The genuinely commonest LEAF, paired with a weekly new-record review
questions.why: A safety net, not a filing system.

questions.q: With edit-rate off for the floor, negotiation:
opts: Moves to pricing rules and the escalation band — where governance wants it
questions.why: The switch relocates discretion; it does not abolish deals.

questions.q: Validate-Against-Purchase-Rate honestly guards against:
opts: The accidental and casual below-cost sale — fuelled by accurate purchase costs
questions.why: State the limitation; fix cost hygiene when it misfires.

questions.q: The same-rate ACTION setting chooses between:
opts: Stop (hard block) and Warning (allow but flag) on a detected drift
questions.why: Ask the client which failure they prefer expensive.

questions.q: Discipline switches should be changed:
opts: As dated, owned policy events — never casually mid-quarter
questions.why: A switch toggled quietly is policy repealed silently.

questions.q: Bundle availability equals:
opts: The scarcest child's coverage — the binding constraint
questions.why: 40 shelves, 3 scanners, 20 printers = 3 packs.

questions.q: A serialized child inside a bundle, on the DN:
opts: Needs no serial — it is bundled
Demands its exact serials on the packed rows as always
questions.why: Bundling changes presentation, never identity discipline.

questions.q: Variant vs bundle vs separate lines:
opts: Variants VARY one thing; bundles COMBINE many; negotiable-per-component stays unsealed as lines
questions.why: The placement test in one sentence.

questions.q: Bundle margin hides because:
opts: The cost is the SUM of children's costs — no single record shows the drift
questions.why: Hence the owned margin file on the repricing cadence.

questions.q: Launching a 50-pack bundle promo is operationally:
opts: A procurement event for the binding-constraint child first
questions.why: Stock the constraint before the promise.

questions.q: A partial bundle return's credit is made non-arbitrary by:
opts: An internal component-value split kept for the sealed parent price
questions.why: Another owned artefact of running bundles seriously.

questions.q: Submitting a blanket order creates:
opts: No reservation and no movement — the commitment is commercial, not logistical
questions.why: Warehouses plan from the drawn orders, not the frame.

questions.q: A customer at 20% drawdown four months into a six-month blanket triggers:
opts: The commercial conversation NOW — extend, revise, or let lapse
questions.why: The blanket turns volume promises into monitorable numbers.

questions.q: A lapsed blanket's ordered-vs-committed record is:
opts: The most honest input to the NEXT negotiation
questions.why: Committed 10,000, drew 7,400 — negotiate from that.

questions.q: When a rep resigns, the Sales Person tree:
opts: Deactivates their node and reassigns accounts — geography in Territory stays put
questions.why: Trees that outlive staff are the point.

questions.q: A 60/40 worked deal is recorded as:
opts: Two Sales Team rows, contributions summing to 100 — credited without double-counting
questions.why: The alternative conventions turn CRM data into politics.

questions.q: Targets by item group make strategy personal because:
opts: The rep weighted toward Services sells Services — mix strategy lands on individuals
questions.why: Aim targets through the product tree.

questions.q: The partner invoices ₦2.4m; your summary says ₦2.1m. You:
opts: Negotiate from the summary; the gap is unstamped deals or misremembered rates
questions.why: The number had a source; the relationship survives BECAUSE of it.

questions.q: The seventh law closes the manual as:
opts: The advanced layer is structure that outlives staff — judgment installed as defaults, visibility, and measurement
questions.why: Make the right thing the default, visible, measured thing.
